exam1.question: What is the main advantage of an in-plane approach for ultrasound-guided needle procedures?

options.text: It eliminates the need for sterile technique
The needle appears as a small echogenic dot
It requires the steepest needle angle
The entire needle shaft and tip can be visualized throughout the procedure

exam1.explanation: With the needle aligned in the plane of the beam, the shaft and tip are seen continuously, improving accuracy and safety. An out-of-plane approach shows only a cross-section of the needle as an echogenic dot.
exam1.hint: Consider which approach keeps the needle within the imaging slice.

exam1.question: Which factor improves needle visibility during ultrasound-guided injection?

options.text: Inserting the needle more parallel to the transducer face
Increasing the overall gain to maximum
Inserting the needle at a steep angle

exam1.explanation: A needle that is closer to parallel with the transducer face reflects more sound back to the transducer, appearing brighter. Steep angles reflect sound away; beam steering or echogenic needles can help when steep angles are needed.
exam1.hint: Specular reflectors are brightest when perpendicular to the beam.

exam1.question: During an ultrasound-guided hip joint aspiration from an anterior approach, which structure lies medially and must be avoided?
exam1.explanation: The anterior hip approach targets the anterior recess at the femoral head-neck junction; the femoral artery, vein, and nerve lie medially and must be identified with Doppler. The sciatic nerve is posterior.
exam1.hint: Recall which vessels lie in front of the hip near the midline of the thigh.

exam1.question: For an ultrasound-guided glenohumeral joint injection from a posterior approach, where is the needle tip targeted?

options.text: Between the posterior labrum and the humeral head

exam1.explanation: In the posterior approach, the needle is directed in plane from lateral to medial into the joint space between the humeral head and the posterior glenoid labrum. The subacromial bursa is not part of the glenohumeral joint.
exam1.hint: The target is the joint space, not a bursa or tendon sheath.

exam1.question: Which complication is associated with a superficial corticosteroid injection into subcutaneous tissue?
exam1.explanation: Corticosteroid deposited superficially can cause subcutaneous fat atrophy and skin depigmentation, particularly in thin tissues. Intratendinous injection can also weaken tendons and increase rupture risk.
exam1.hint: Consider what happens when a depot steroid is deposited too superficially in a thin patient.

exam1.question: What is a disadvantage of spatial compound imaging in MSK ultrasound?

options.text: It can reduce diagnostically useful shadowing and enhancement

exam1.explanation: Spatial compounding averages multiple steered frames, reducing speckle and anisotropy but also diminishing posterior shadowing behind calcifications and enhancement behind cysts. Turning it off can help characterize these features.
exam1.hint: Averaging frames from different angles fills in artifacts that sometimes help diagnosis.

exam1.question: Which tool is most useful for documenting the full extent of a large muscle tear or the retraction gap of a tendon?
exam1.explanation: Extended field-of-view imaging stitches together frames to display and measure structures longer than the transducer footprint. Harmonic imaging improves contrast but does not extend the field.
exam1.hint: The finding to document is longer than any single image can display.

exam1.question: A 30-year-old cyclist fell directly onto the point of his shoulder. Coronal sonography over the top of the shoulder shows a widened joint between the clavicle and acromion, with the distal clavicle displaced superiorly relative to the acromion and adjacent hematoma. The coracoclavicular distance is greater than on the other side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: A direct fall on the shoulder that widens the acromioclavicular joint and elevates the distal clavicle, with an increased coracoclavicular distance, indicates acromioclavicular joint separation with coracoclavicular ligament injury. Distal clavicular osteolysis is a chronic overuse condition with cortical erosion, not acute superior displacement after trauma.
exam1.hint: Think about which ligaments hold the clavicle down to the scapula and what happens when they fail.

exam1.question: Where is a small elbow joint effusion most readily detected with sonography?

options.text: Medial elbow over the ulnar collateral ligament during valgus stress
Lateral elbow over the common extensor origin with the forearm pronated
Posterior olecranon recess with the elbow flexed about 45 to 90 degrees
Antecubital fossa superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis

exam1.explanation: The posterior olecranon recess is the most dependent and distensible part of the elbow joint, and flexion displaces fluid into it, elevating the posterior fat pad. The antecubital fossa superficial to the aponeurosis is outside the joint capsule, so fluid there would not represent an effusion.
exam1.hint: Think about the recess that also lifts the posterior fat pad on a lateral radiograph.

exam1.question: During infant hip sonography using the coronal view, what minimum percentage of femoral head coverage by the bony acetabulum is generally considered normal?
exam1.explanation: In the coronal view, the bony acetabulum normally covers at least half of the femoral head; coverage below about 50 percent suggests a shallow acetabulum or subluxation. Values in the 40 to 50 percent range are borderline in very young infants and are not considered clearly normal.
exam1.hint: Picture how much of the round cartilaginous femoral head the normal acetabular roof encloses on the coronal image.

exam1.question: A 12-year-old basketball player has anterior knee pain with jumping. Sonography shows fragmentation and irregularity of the inferior pole of the patella with a thickened, hypoechoic proximal patellar tendon. The tibial tuberosity appears normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease is a traction apophysitis at the inferior pole of the patella in adolescents, with fragmentation and proximal patellar tendon thickening. Osgood-Schlatter disease involves the distal tendon at the tibial tuberosity, which is normal here.
exam1.hint: Locate the abnormality: proximal or distal end of the patellar tendon.

exam1.question: A 14-year-old girl has medial midfoot pain and a bony prominence that rubs in her skates. Sonography shows the posterior tibial tendon inserting onto a separate ossicle medial to the navicular, with an irregular hypoechoic junction between the ossicle and navicular and local hyperemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: An accessory navicular is an ossicle at the posterior tibial tendon insertion; stress across its fibrocartilaginous junction (synchondrosis) causes pain, irregularity, and hyperemia. A navicular stress fracture typically involves the central dorsal navicular body, not a separate ossicle within the tendon insertion.
exam1.hint: The tendon is attaching to an extra bone rather than the navicular itself.

exam1.question: A 30-year-old man cannot make an OK sign because he cannot flex the thumb interphalangeal joint or the index finger distal interphalangeal joint. Sensation is normal. Sonography of which muscle would most likely show denervation changes such as increased echogenicity?
exam1.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve is a pure motor branch of the median nerve that supplies the flexor pollicis longus, the index flexor digitorum profundus, and the pronator quadratus, which is easy to image over the distal forearm. The abductor pollicis brevis is supplied by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve at the wrist, which is affected in carpal tunnel syndrome instead.
exam1.hint: The deficit points to a pure motor branch of the median nerve in the forearm.

exam1.question: A 50-year-old man with long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes and end-stage renal disease has acute severe thigh pain and swelling. He is afebrile with a normal white blood cell count. Sonography shows swollen, hypoechoic quadriceps muscle with preserved but separated fibers, no drainable collection, no gas, and little internal flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: Diabetic myonecrosis occurs in patients with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes and microvascular disease, typically in the thigh, as painful swelling of muscle with preserved architecture, no abscess, and reduced flow. Pyomyositis would usually cause fever and a drainable collection with peripheral hyperemia.
exam1.hint: Note the absence of fever, gas, and a drainable collection in a patient with severe small-vessel disease.

exam1.question: When imaging a tendon at a depth of 1.5 cm with a high-frequency linear transducer, where should the focal zone be placed?

options.text: At the skin surface to sharpen the near field
At or just below the level of the tendon
At the deepest part of the image field
Well above the tendon to reduce reverberation

exam1.explanation: Lateral resolution is best where the beam is narrowest, so the focal zone should be placed at or just below the structure of interest. Placing the focus at the deepest part of the field widens the beam at the tendon depth and blurs fine fibrillar detail.
exam1.hint: The beam is narrowest at the focus, so put it where you need the best detail.

exam1.question: A 34-year-old man felt a pop in the front of his chest and armpit while bench pressing. He has bruising over the upper arm and loss of the normal anterior axillary fold. Which portion of the injured muscle is most commonly torn?

options.text: The sternal head of the pectoralis major at its humeral insertion or myotendinous junction
The clavicular head of the pectoralis major at its origin on the medial clavicle
The pectoralis minor at its insertion on the coracoid process
The long head of the biceps at the supraglenoid tubercle

exam1.explanation: Pectoralis major tears from eccentric loading during bench press usually involve the sternal (inferior) head at its humeral tendon insertion or myotendinous junction, producing loss of the anterior axillary fold. Clavicular head origin tears are uncommon, and pectoralis minor injury would not efface the axillary fold.
exam1.hint: Think about which portion of the muscle is under the greatest eccentric stretch as the bar is lowered to the chest.

exam1.question: A 52-year-old weightlifter fell onto an outstretched hand and now has weakness of elbow extension. Sonography of the posterior elbow shows a fluid-filled gap at the olecranon with a retracted, wavy tendon and a small shadowing echogenic fragment within the proximal stump. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: A retracted tendon with a gap at the olecranon and a bony flake in the stump indicates avulsion of the distal triceps tendon, which commonly takes a cortical fragment with it. Olecranon bursitis is a superficial fluid collection with the tendon intact, and it would not cause weakness of extension.
exam1.hint: The echogenic fragment travels with the retracted tendon away from its insertion.

exam1.question: During dynamic infant hip sonography, which maneuver tests whether a located hip can be displaced out of the acetabulum?

options.text: Ortolani maneuver: abduction of the flexed hip with an anterior lift of the femur
Barlow maneuver: adduction of the flexed hip with gentle posterior pressure
Galeazzi test: comparing knee heights with both hips and knees flexed
Thompson test: squeezing the calf to observe passive plantarflexion

exam1.explanation: The Barlow maneuver adducts the flexed hip while pushing posteriorly to see whether a seated femoral head can be subluxated or dislocated, and sonography shows the head moving posterolaterally. The Ortolani maneuver does the opposite, reducing an already dislocated hip with abduction and an anterior lift.
exam1.hint: One maneuver tries to push the head out; the other tries to bring it back in.

exam1.question: How should the knee be positioned and scanned to measure femoral trochlear cartilage thickness?

options.text: Knee fully extended with a longitudinal scan below the patella
Patient prone with a transverse scan of the popliteal fossa
Knee extended with a coronal scan of the medial joint line
Knee maximally flexed with a transverse scan above the patella

exam1.explanation: Maximal knee flexion moves the patella distally and exposes the femoral trochlea, allowing a transverse suprapatellar scan to show the anechoic cartilage over the condyles. With the knee extended, the patella covers the trochlea and the cartilage cannot be measured.
exam1.hint: The patella must be moved out of the way to expose the trochlear groove.

exam1.question: After an eversion ankle injury, which ligament complex is evaluated by placing the transducer with one end on the medial malleolus and fanning toward the navicular, talus, and calcaneus?
exam1.explanation: The deltoid ligament fans from the medial malleolus to the navicular, talus, and calcaneus and is stressed by eversion injuries. The spring ligament is also medial but runs from the sustentaculum tali to the navicular, not from the malleolus, and the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments arise from the lateral malleolus and are injured by inversion.
exam1.hint: Consider which medial ligament actually originates from the malleolus rather than from the hindfoot bones.

exam1.question: When the sciatic nerve is followed distally in short axis, where does it typically divide into the tibial and common peroneal nerves?

options.text: In the distal thigh near the apex of the popliteal fossa
At the greater sciatic notch just below the piriformis
At the level of the fibular neck
At the level of the ischial tuberosity

exam1.explanation: The tibial and common peroneal components usually separate in the distal thigh near the apex of the popliteal fossa, although a higher division is a known variant. The fibular neck is where the common peroneal nerve itself divides into deep and superficial branches.
exam1.hint: Follow the nerve down the posterior thigh until it reaches the top of the knee region.

exam1.question: Which sonographic appearance is most typical of cellulitis without abscess?

options.text: Thickened, hyperechoic subcutaneous fat with branching anechoic fluid strands and no focal collection
A well-defined anechoic collection with posterior enhancement and debris that swirls with pressure
Echogenic foci with dirty posterior shadowing along the deep fascia
An ovoid hypoechoic dermal lesion with a thin tract extending to the skin surface

exam1.explanation: Cellulitis thickens and brightens the subcutaneous fat, with interlobular fluid producing a cobblestone pattern but no focal fluid collection; the pattern is not specific and needs clinical correlation. A swirling anechoic collection with posterior enhancement indicates an abscess that may need drainage.
exam1.hint: Think about how edema distributes between fat lobules before any pus has formed.

exam1.question: Compared with healthy tendons, how do tendinopathic tendons such as the Achilles most often appear on shear wave elastography?

options.text: Stiffer, with higher shear wave velocity throughout
Unchanged, because elastography cannot detect tendinopathy
Softer, with lower shear wave velocity
Stiffer only at the enthesis and normal elsewhere

exam1.explanation: Tendinopathy disrupts the organized collagen and increases ground substance and water, so affected tendons usually show reduced stiffness and lower shear wave velocity. Higher stiffness is not the typical finding, although measurements vary with tendon tension and joint position, which must be standardized.
exam1.hint: Think about how disorganized collagen and added water change tissue firmness.

exam1.question: When assessing fatty atrophy of the supraspinatus muscle with sonography, its echogenicity in the supraspinous fossa is commonly compared with which overlying reference muscle?
exam1.explanation: The trapezius lies directly over the supraspinatus in the same field of view, so a supraspinatus that is brighter than the trapezius, with poorly seen pennate pattern and central tendon, indicates fatty infiltration. The subscapularis is on the anterior scapula and cannot be compared side by side in the same image.
exam1.hint: A useful reference muscle must appear in the same image so depth and gain settings are identical.

exam1.question: A 27-year-old fell onto an outstretched hand and has dorsal wrist pain with normal radiographs. A dorsal transverse scan just distal to Lister tubercle shows a disrupted intercarpal ligament, and the interval between the two carpal bones it joins widens when the patient clenches the fist. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam1.explanation: The dorsal segment of the scapholunate ligament is seen just distal to Lister tubercle, and disruption with dynamic widening of the scapholunate interval during fist clenching indicates a tear. The lunotriquetral ligament lies more ulnarly, between the lunate and triquetrum.
exam1.hint: Use Lister tubercle as the landmark and recall which proximal carpal row bones lie directly beyond it.

exam1.question: A newborn with breech presentation has a normal hip examination. Why is sonographic screening of the hips generally deferred until about 4 to 6 weeks of age?

options.text: Physiologic laxity and immaturity in the first weeks often resolve and can cause false-positive results
The femoral head ossification center blocks visualization of the acetabulum before 6 weeks
High-frequency linear transducers cannot resolve the cartilaginous femoral head in newborns
Radiographs are more accurate than sonography during the first month of life

exam1.explanation: Mild laxity and acetabular immaturity are common in the first weeks of life and usually resolve, so scanning too early produces many false-positive studies; a stable clinical exam allows deferral to about 4 to 6 weeks. The femoral head ossification center appears later, at several months, and it limits sonography only in older infants.
exam1.hint: Consider what normally happens to newborn hip laxity during the first several weeks.

exam1.question: A 55-year-old man has chronic painless swelling of the knee. Sonography shows a large suprapatellar effusion containing frond-like, villous hyperechoic synovial projections that sway with compression and show minimal Doppler flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (pigmented villonodular synovitis)

exam1.explanation: Lipoma arborescens is fatty villous proliferation of the synovium, seen as hyperechoic fronds floating in an effusion, most often in the suprapatellar recess. Tenosynovial giant cell tumor usually forms hypoechoic, vascular synovial masses rather than bright fatty fronds.
exam1.hint: Bright, tree-like synovial fronds suggest fat within the synovium.

exam2.question: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes has rapidly spreading thigh pain out of proportion to visible redness, fever, and hypotension. Sonography shows fluid along the deep fascia and echogenic foci with dirty posterior shadowing within the soft tissues. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Fluid tracking along the deep fascia with soft tissue gas, in a patient with sepsis and severe pain, suggests necrotizing fasciitis, a surgical emergency. Simple cellulitis does not cause gas or deep fascial fluid.
exam2.hint: Consider which tissue plane the fluid follows and how systemically ill the patient is.

exam2.question: A 71-year-old man reports a slapping gait and a painless lump on the front of his ankle that began after he tripped. Sonography shows an empty sheath anterior to the medial ankle with a retracted, bulbous tendon stump proximal to the extensor retinaculum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Tibialis anterior rupture typically occurs in older adults with minor trauma, causing foot slap and a pseudomass from the retracted stump. A common peroneal nerve palsy can also cause foot slap, but the tendon would be intact.
exam2.hint: The lump is the clue: a retracted stump forms a pseudomass.

exam2.question: After a first-time anterior glenohumeral dislocation in a 22-year-old man, the sonographer scans the posterior humeral head in the transverse plane. Which finding is most expected?

options.text: A cortical defect of the anteromedial humeral head
A cortical notch or flattening of the posterolateral humeral head
Calcification within the teres minor tendon

exam2.explanation: Anterior dislocation impacts the posterolateral humeral head against the anterior glenoid rim, producing a Hill-Sachs defect seen as a cortical notch. An anteromedial head defect (reverse Hill-Sachs) follows posterior dislocation.
exam2.hint: Picture where the humeral head strikes the glenoid rim when it is displaced anteriorly.

exam2.question: A 63-year-old man felt a pop in his shoulder while lifting a heavy bag and now has a bulge in the lower anterior arm. Short-axis imaging shows an empty bicipital groove with no tendon visible medially over the lesser tuberosity, and a wavy tendon stump with hematoma lies in the distal arm. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Medial dislocation of the long head biceps tendon
Distal biceps tendon rupture at the radial tuberosity
Musculotendinous tear of the pectoralis major
Rupture of the long head biceps tendon

exam2.explanation: An empty groove with no tendon displaced medially, plus a retracted stump in the arm and a Popeye bulge, indicates proximal long head biceps rupture. Dislocation would show the tendon displaced medially over or within the subscapularis.
exam2.hint: An empty groove has two explanations; decide which one the absence of a medially displaced tendon supports.
keywords: empty bicipital groove with no tendon

exam2.question: A 46-year-old woman has a slowly growing, painless, firm mass on the volar index finger. Sonography shows a solid hypoechoic lobulated mass abutting the flexor tendon, with internal Doppler flow, that does not move with the tendon during finger flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath
Ganglion cyst of the flexor tendon sheath

exam2.explanation: Giant cell tumor of the tendon sheath is the most common solid hand mass, appearing as a solid hypoechoic vascular mass beside a tendon that does not glide with it. A ganglion is anechoic and avascular, and a glomus tumor is typically small, subungual, and painful.
exam2.hint: Weigh solid versus cystic, painless versus painful, and finger-shaft versus nail-bed location.

exam2.question: A 59-year-old woman fell onto her shoulder; radiographs were read as normal, but she has persistent pain and weakness. Sonography shows an intact supraspinatus tendon with a small step-off in the cortex of the greater tuberosity and adjacent hypoechoic hematoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Hill-Sachs impaction of the posterolateral humeral head
Full-thickness supraspinatus tear at the footprint
Calcific enthesopathy of the supraspinatus insertion

exam2.explanation: A cortical step-off with intact overlying tendon after a fall indicates a greater tuberosity fracture, which is often occult on radiographs and mimics cuff tear clinically. A full-thickness tear would show tendon discontinuity rather than an intact tendon.
exam2.hint: The tendon is intact, so focus on what the cortical contour abnormality represents.

exam2.question: A 50-year-old man has numbness of the fourth and fifth fingers and weak grip. Which sonographic finding at the elbow most supports ulnar neuropathy at the cubital tunnel?

options.text: Ulnar nerve CSA of 6 mm2 at the medial epicondyle with a preserved fascicular pattern
Hypoechoic swelling of the ulnar nerve at the medial epicondyle with a CSA of about 10 mm2 or more
The ulnar nerve lying posterior to the medial epicondyle with the elbow extended
Equal ulnar nerve CSA at the medial epicondyle and in the mid arm

exam2.explanation: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is supported by focal hypoechoic enlargement at the medial epicondyle, with a CSA of roughly 10 mm2 or more (published cutoffs range from about 8 to 10 mm2) or a clear increase relative to the arm. A nerve posterior to the epicondyle in extension is its normal position, and equal size along the nerve argues against focal entrapment.
exam2.hint: Recall the approximate upper limit of normal ulnar nerve size at the elbow.

exam2.question: A 45-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is scanned at the second MCP joint. By OMERACT definition, which finding qualifies as a bone erosion?

options.text: A cortical irregularity seen only in the longitudinal plane
A bony spur at the joint margin
An intra-articular discontinuity of the bone surface seen in two perpendicular planes
A hyperechoic band on the cartilage surface

exam2.explanation: OMERACT defines an erosion as an intra-articular discontinuity of the bone surface visible in two perpendicular planes, which helps avoid mistaking normal cortical irregularity for an erosion. A marginal spur is an osteophyte, typical of osteoarthritis.
exam2.hint: Recall that OMERACT definitions specify both the location of the defect and how it must be confirmed.

exam2.question: A complete hamstring tear has retracted beyond the length of the transducer footprint. Which tool best documents the retraction distance in a single view?
exam2.explanation: Extended field-of-view imaging stitches sequential frames into one long panoramic image, allowing measurement of a tendon gap longer than the transducer footprint. Harmonic and compound imaging improve image quality but do not lengthen the field of view.
exam2.hint: The problem is the length of the area to be shown, not image quality.

exam2.question: While scanning the supraspinatus in long axis, the sonographer sees a hypoechoic area where the tendon curves down to the greater tuberosity. What should be done before calling it tendinosis or tear?

options.text: Increase the overall gain until the area appears echogenic
Switch to a lower-frequency curvilinear transducer
Heel-toe the transducer so the beam is perpendicular to the fibers at that segment
Apply firm compression to flatten the tendon

exam2.explanation: Curving tendon fibers at an insertion are prone to anisotropy, which artificially darkens them when the beam is not perpendicular; heel-toe rocking in long axis corrects it. Raising gain does not correct an angle-dependent artifact.
exam2.hint: Consider what happens to fiber echogenicity where a tendon changes direction.

exam2.question: A 25-year-old competitive weightlifter has activity-related pain at the top of the shoulder without trauma. Sonography shows cortical irregularity and erosion of the distal clavicle, a widened acromioclavicular joint, and capsular distension, while the acromion cortex is smooth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Repetitive microtrauma in weightlifters causes resorption of the distal clavicle with erosive irregularity and joint widening, sparing the acromion. Septic arthritis is possible but would be expected with systemic signs and rapid onset rather than chronic training-related pain.
exam2.hint: Consider which repetitive loading injury selectively affects one side of this joint.

exam2.question: In short-axis imaging of a normal Achilles tendon, thin vertical shadows extend posteriorly from both tendon edges. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Edge (refractive) shadowing artifact at the curved tendon margins

exam2.explanation: Refraction at the curved margins of a rounded structure creates thin edge shadows that can mimic tears or calcification. True tears would be reproducible in long axis with fiber discontinuity.
exam2.hint: Ask whether a tear or calcification would look like this in long axis and at both tendon margins at once.

exam2.question: A 13-year-old boy who plays soccer has a painful prominence below the knee. Sonography shows fragmentation of the tibial tuberosity ossification center, thickening of the distal patellar tendon, and fluid in the deep infrapatellar bursa. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tibial tuberosity avulsion fracture with displacement

exam2.explanation: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity in adolescents, with fragmentation, distal patellar tendon thickening, and deep infrapatellar bursitis. Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease affects the inferior patellar pole instead.
exam2.hint: Locate the abnormality at the proximal versus distal end of the patellar tendon.

exam2.question: A 19-year-old ballet dancer has posteromedial ankle pain in the en pointe position. Sonography shows fluid and synovial thickening around the flexor hallucis longus tendon behind the talus with an os trigonum, while the ankle joint has no effusion. Why is the absence of an ankle effusion important?

options.text: It excludes an os trigonum syndrome
It indicates a complete FHL rupture
The FHL sheath often communicates with the ankle joint, so isolated sheath fluid without joint effusion is more significant
It proves the fluid is from a ganglion of the posterior talofibular ligament

exam2.explanation: Because the flexor hallucis longus sheath communicates with the ankle joint in a sizable minority of people, sheath fluid may merely reflect a joint effusion; disproportionate fluid without effusion suggests true tenosynovitis. Os trigonum syndrome often coexists with FHL tenosynovitis in dancers rather than being excluded.
exam2.hint: Consider where fluid in this particular sheath can come from.

exam2.question: A 31-year-old woman has a slowly enlarging mass near the knee that appears hypoechoic with posterior enhancement, suggesting a ganglion. Which additional finding should prevent a diagnosis of ganglion and prompt further workup?

options.text: A thin neck toward the joint
Internal vascularity on color or power Doppler

exam2.explanation: Ganglia are avascular, so internal flow indicates a solid lesion such as synovial sarcoma, which can mimic a cyst with posterior enhancement. A lobulated contour and a neck to the joint are typical ganglion features.
exam2.hint: Consider which features ganglia share with cyst-like solid tumors, and which they do not.

exam2.question: A 280-lb patient needs an ultrasound-guided hip joint aspiration through the anterior approach. Which transducer is most appropriate?

options.text: High-frequency hockey-stick linear transducer (about 15 to 18 MHz)
Phased-array transducer at 7 MHz with a standoff pad

exam2.explanation: Deep structures in a large patient require the penetration of a low-frequency curvilinear transducer. A high-frequency hockey-stick transducer is ideal for fingers and superficial structures but cannot reach the hip joint in a large patient.
exam2.hint: Depth of the target determines the frequency trade-off.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old man has progressive foot drop with weakness of ankle dorsiflexion. Sonography at the fibular neck shows a tubular, multilobulated anechoic structure within the common peroneal nerve, with a thin branch extending to the proximal tibiofibular joint. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Extraneural ganglion compressing the tibial nerve
Schwannoma of the common peroneal nerve
Intraneural ganglion cyst of the common peroneal nerve

exam2.explanation: Intraneural ganglia of the peroneal nerve arise from the proximal tibiofibular joint and track along the articular branch into the nerve sheath; identifying that connection is critical to prevent recurrence. A schwannoma is solid rather than tubular and cystic.
exam2.hint: Follow the thin branch back to its joint of origin.

exam2.question: A 56-year-old man with Dupuytren contracture has firm nodules in the arch of both feet. Sonography shows well-defined fusiform hypoechoic nodules within the mid-portion of the plantar fascia, sparing the calcaneal origin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Plantar fibromatosis produces nodular hypoechoic thickening in the mid-fascia, often bilateral and associated with palmar fibromatosis. Plantar fasciitis affects the calcaneal origin rather than the midfoot.
exam2.hint: Note the association with a hand condition and where along the fascia the nodules lie.

exam2.question: A 9-year-old with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a soft, enlarging thigh swelling. Sonography shows a large infiltrative lesion composed of multiple tortuous enlarged hypoechoic fascicles along a nerve, resembling a bag of worms. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Plexiform neurofibromas, essentially diagnostic of NF1, involve long segments and branches of a nerve, producing multiple enlarged tortuous fascicles. A venous malformation would be compressible with slow venous flow and possible phleboliths.
exam2.hint: The lesion follows nerve fascicles, and the patient has a known syndrome.

exam2.question: A 44-year-old carpenter has lateral elbow pain worsened by gripping. Sonography shows a thickened, hypoechoic common extensor origin with intratendinous Doppler flow and small calcifications; the radial collateral ligament is intact. The fibers of which tendon are most typically involved?
exam2.explanation: Lateral epicondylopathy primarily involves the deep anterior fibers of the extensor carpi radialis brevis at the common extensor origin. The extensor carpi radialis longus originates more proximally from the supracondylar ridge rather than the common origin.
exam2.hint: Recall which wrist extensor contributes the deep anterior portion of the common extensor origin.

exam2.question: A 37-year-old man has wrist drop and numbness over the dorsal first web space six weeks after a midshaft humeral fracture. Which nerve should be scanned for entrapment in callus along the posterior humerus?

options.text: Ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel
Median nerve at the pronator teres
Radial nerve in the spiral groove

exam2.explanation: The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove along the posterior humeral shaft and is the nerve most often injured with midshaft humeral fractures, causing wrist drop and dorsal web space numbness. Ulnar and median nerves do not produce wrist drop.
exam2.hint: Match the motor deficit and the sensory area to a nerve that runs close to the fracture site.

exam2.question: A 63-year-old woman has pain under the second metatarsal head, and the second toe is drifting dorsally and medially. Long-axis plantar sonography shows a hypoechoic defect where a fibrocartilaginous structure deep to the flexor tendons attaches to the base of the proximal phalanx, with joint instability on dorsal translation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Morton neuroma of the second intermetatarsal space
Freiberg infraction of the second metatarsal head
Plantar plate tear of the second metatarsophalangeal joint

exam2.explanation: The plantar plate is a fibrocartilaginous stabilizer deep to the flexor tendons, and tears at its phalangeal attachment are common at the second MTP joint, leading to toe deviation and instability. Freiberg infraction is osteonecrosis that flattens the metatarsal head itself.
exam2.hint: Identify the fibrocartilaginous stabilizer of the lesser MTP joint that lies deep to the flexor tendons.

exam2.question: A 35-year-old man with neurofibromatosis type 1 has a known neurofibroma in the thigh. Which change on follow-up sonography is most concerning for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor?

options.text: A stable size with a central hyperechoic target
Fusiform shape with a nerve entering and exiting centrally
Rapid growth with new pain, ill-defined margins, and heterogeneous necrotic areas
Posterior acoustic enhancement without change in size

exam2.explanation: Rapid enlargement, new pain, irregular margins, and internal heterogeneity or necrosis raise concern for malignant transformation, which warrants MRI and biopsy. A stable target sign is a reassuring benign feature.
exam2.hint: Concerning findings combine clinical change with loss of benign imaging features.

exam2.question: A sonographer is searching for a 2 mm calcification in a tendon. Why might turning off spatial compound imaging help?

options.text: Compounding averages multiple beam angles and can fill in the posterior shadowing that helps identify small calcifications
Compounding increases anisotropy, making tendons too dark
Compounding prevents color Doppler from functioning
Compounding increases penetration and degrades near-field resolution only

exam2.explanation: Spatial compounding reduces speckle and anisotropy but also reduces acoustic shadowing behind small calcifications or foreign bodies, so turning it off can make them more conspicuous. Compounding actually reduces anisotropy rather than increasing it.
exam2.hint: Consider the trade-offs of averaging multiple beam angles into one image.

exam2.question: A 34-year-old police officer has numbness over the dorsoradial hand after wearing a tight watch strap. Sonography shows focal swelling of a small superficial nerve over the distal radius, where it emerges from beneath the brachioradialis tendon into the subcutaneous tissue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Compression of the superficial radial nerve by tight watchbands or handcuffs causes dorsoradial hand numbness, known as Wartenberg syndrome or cheiralgia paresthetica. The posterior interosseous nerve is purely motor and does not cause numbness.
exam2.hint: Map the numb skin area to the nerve that supplies it and the point where a strap could press on it.

exam2.question: A 41-year-old woman has a slowly enlarging, tender mass behind the knee with tingling in the sole when it is pressed. Sonography shows a well-defined oval hypoechoic mass with posterior enhancement and internal flow, located eccentrically along the tibial nerve, with the nerve fascicles displaced around its periphery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Schwannomas arise eccentrically from the nerve sheath and displace fascicles to the periphery, often with posterior enhancement despite being solid. Neurofibromas tend to be central and fusiform, with the nerve entering and exiting centrally.
exam2.hint: Note whether the nerve fascicles pass through the center of the mass or around its edge.

exam2.question: A 55-year-old man with serum urate of 10.2 mg/dL has a firm swelling at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Sonography shows a heterogeneous hyperechoic aggregate with a thin anechoic rim and an adjacent cortical erosion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Tophi appear as heterogeneous hyperechoic aggregates, sometimes described as wet sugar clumps, with an anechoic rim, often beside erosions at the first MTP joint in hyperuricemic patients. A bunion bursa is a fluid-filled sac over the medial first metatarsal head.
exam2.hint: Focus on the echotexture of the aggregate and its rim, and what lies next to it.

exam2.question: A 40-year-old man with psoriasis has posterior heel pain. Sonography of the Achilles insertion shows thickening, hypoechogenicity, an enthesophyte, and a cortical erosion. Which additional finding most supports active enthesitis?

options.text: Fluid in the superficial calcaneal bursa
Doppler signal at the enthesis within 2 mm of the bone cortex
Increased tendon thickness 5 cm above the insertion

exam2.explanation: In spondyloarthritis, Doppler signal at the enthesis close to the bony cortex indicates active inflammation, while enthesophytes and erosions may reflect chronic damage. Thickening 5 cm above the insertion is a midportion finding, not an enthesis finding.
exam2.hint: Distinguish markers of current inflammation from markers of past damage.

exam2.question: A 60-year-old man with diabetic polyneuropathy has symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome. Because his nerves are diffusely enlarged, the sonographer measures the median nerve CSA at both the carpal tunnel inlet and the pronator quadratus level. Which result most supports focal entrapment?

options.text: A wrist-to-forearm CSA ratio of exactly 1.0
A forearm CSA larger than the wrist CSA
A wrist-to-forearm CSA ratio greater than about 1.4

exam2.explanation: When nerves are diffusely enlarged, the ratio of inlet CSA to forearm CSA helps isolate focal swelling; a ratio above about 1.4 is the commonly cited cutoff for carpal tunnel syndrome. Equal enlargement at both sites suggests generalized neuropathy rather than focal entrapment.
exam2.hint: Focal entrapment causes swelling at one site relative to a proximal internal reference.

exam2.question: A 29-year-old woman training for a marathon has focal forefoot pain and normal radiographs. Sonography over the second metatarsal shaft shows a short segment of elevated periosteum with a hypoechoic cuff of tissue, focal cortical irregularity, and surrounding hyperemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Periosteal elevation with a hypoechoic cuff, cortical irregularity, and hyperemia over the metatarsal shaft indicates a stress fracture, which ultrasound can detect before radiographic change. Freiberg infraction involves the metatarsal head, not the shaft.
exam2.hint: Radiographs often lag behind early bone stress injury.

exam2.question: In a 50-year-old man with inflammatory arthritis, the wrist shows hypoechoic intra-articular material. Which feature identifies it as synovial hypertrophy rather than effusion?

options.text: It is anechoic and displaces with transducer pressure
It is poorly compressible and nondisplaceable, and may show Doppler signal
It layers dependently with a fluid-fluid level

exam2.explanation: Per OMERACT, synovial hypertrophy is abnormal intra-articular tissue that is nondisplaceable and poorly compressible and may show Doppler signal, whereas effusion is displaceable and compressible. Layering and enhancement are fluid behaviors.
exam2.hint: Apply gentle pressure mentally: tissue and fluid respond differently.

exam2.question: A 25-year-old man cut his volar wrist on glass three months ago and has persistent numbness in the median nerve distribution. Sonography shows a fusiform hypoechoic swelling of the median nerve at the scar, with the epineurium and some fascicles continuous through the swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A fusiform swelling at the injury site with preserved nerve continuity is a neuroma in continuity, whereas complete transection shows a gap with a bulbous end-bulb neuroma. Lipofibromatous hamartoma is a congenital fatty infiltration with a cable-like appearance.
exam2.hint: Decide whether the nerve is still intact across the injury site.

exam2.question: A 35-year-old woman who injects drugs has a red, painful forearm swelling and fever. Sonography shows a hypoechoic collection with internal debris that swirls with transducer pressure and peripheral hyperemia, surrounded by edematous fat. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A collection with mobile swirling debris and peripheral hyperemia is an abscess that may need drainage, whereas cellulitis shows only edematous, cobblestoned fat without a collection. Swirling with pressure indicates fluid content, not solid tissue.
exam2.hint: The response to transducer pressure tells you whether the contents are liquid.

exam2.question: Six weeks after a nondisplaced distal radius fracture treated in a cast, a 64-year-old woman suddenly cannot extend the thumb interphalangeal joint. Sonography shows an empty tendon sheath just ulnar to Lister tubercle with a retracted stump proximally. Which tendon has ruptured?
exam2.explanation: The extensor pollicis longus runs in the third compartment, turning around Lister tubercle, and is prone to delayed attritional or ischemic rupture after a distal radius fracture, even a nondisplaced one. The extensor pollicis brevis extends only to the proximal phalanx and runs in the first compartment.
exam2.hint: Use Lister tubercle as the pulley landmark for the tendon that reaches the distal thumb phalanx.

exam2.question: A 41-year-old man has chronic lateral ankle pain after recurrent sprains. Short-axis sonography behind the lateral malleolus shows the peroneus brevis flattened into a C shape partially wrapped around the peroneus longus, with a longitudinal cleft dividing it. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Longitudinal split tear of the peroneus brevis

exam2.explanation: A peroneus brevis split tear shows a flattened, boomerang-shaped tendon divided by a cleft, often with the longus pushing between the halves against the fibular groove. An accessory peroneus quartus appears as an additional muscle or tendon rather than a split.
exam2.hint: The tendon nearest the fibula is compressed between bone and the other tendon.

exam2.question: A 20-year-old soccer player has anterior thigh pain after a forceful kick. Short-axis sonography of the proximal rectus femoris shows a hypoechoic halo of edema surrounding the central echogenic aponeurosis, creating a target appearance. Which injury is most likely?

options.text: Avulsion of the direct head from the anterior inferior iliac spine
Strain of the indirect head at the central myotendinous junction
Rupture of the sartorius from the anterior superior iliac spine
Vastus intermedius contusion against the femur

exam2.explanation: The indirect head of the rectus femoris continues into the muscle as a central aponeurosis, and strains there produce a characteristic bull's-eye or target pattern of edema around it. Direct head avulsion would show a bony fragment at the anterior inferior iliac spine.
exam2.hint: Locate the injury relative to the central tendon that runs within the muscle belly.

exam2.question: Before an ultrasound-guided steroid injection for De Quervain tenosynovitis in a 42-year-old woman, the sonographer sees a thin hypoechoic vertical band dividing the first dorsal compartment into two subcompartments. Why is this finding important?

options.text: It indicates a longitudinal split tear that contraindicates injection
It represents the radial artery, which must be avoided by switching to the second compartment
An intracompartmental septum can isolate the extensor pollicis brevis, so each subcompartment may need to be injected
It is an anisotropy artifact that disappears with heel-toe maneuvering

exam2.explanation: An intracompartmental septum is a common variant that separates the extensor pollicis brevis subcompartment; failure to inject both subcompartments is a recognized cause of treatment failure. Split tears appear as clefts within a tendon, not as a band between tendons.
exam2.hint: Think about why injectate placed in one tendon sheath might not reach both tendons.

exam2.question: A 27-year-old volleyball player has posterior shoulder ache and weakness of external rotation. The infraspinatus is small and hyperechoic while the supraspinatus is normal, and a lobulated anechoic cyst sits at the spinoglenoid notch. Which associated finding should be sought?

options.text: Medial dislocation of the long head biceps tendon

exam2.explanation: A paralabral cyst at the spinoglenoid notch usually arises from a posterosuperior labral tear and compresses the suprascapular nerve distal to the supraspinatus branch, so only the infraspinatus atrophies. A cyst at the suprascapular notch would affect both muscles.
exam2.hint: Paralabral cysts form where joint fluid escapes through a defect; think about where that defect lies.

exam2.question: A 33-year-old man fell from a ladder onto his knee. Radiographs are pending. Sonography of the suprapatellar recess shows a large effusion with a horizontal level: a hyperechoic layer floating on top, with hypoechoic fluid and dependent echogenic debris below. What does this most strongly indicate?

options.text: Simple hemarthrosis from a cruciate ligament sprain

exam2.explanation: A floating hyperechoic fat layer above blood indicates marrow fat released into the joint, which means an intra-articular fracture such as a tibial plateau fracture. A simple hemarthrosis lacks the floating fat layer.
exam2.hint: Ask which components of blood and marrow separate by density in a joint.

exam2.question: A 52-year-old woman reports nocturnal numbness of the thumb, index, and middle fingers. At the carpal tunnel inlet (pisiform level), the median nerve measures 14 mm2 and is hypoechoic with loss of fascicular detail. How should this measurement be interpreted?

options.text: Normal, because enlargement is not diagnostic until the nerve exceeds 20 mm2
Enlarged, supporting carpal tunnel syndrome, because it exceeds the commonly used threshold of about 10 mm2
Normal, because measurements at the inlet are routinely larger than in the forearm
Nondiagnostic, because CSA must be measured at the hook of hamate only

exam2.explanation: Median nerve CSA at the inlet above roughly 10 mm2 (published cutoffs range from about 9 to 12 mm2) supports carpal tunnel syndrome, and 14 mm2 is clearly enlarged. The inlet at the pisiform is the standard and most sensitive measurement site.
exam2.hint: Compare the value with the widely taught upper limit of normal at the tunnel inlet.

exam2.question: A 62-year-old woman has lateral hip pain that is worse when lying on that side and climbing stairs. Sonography shows a thickened hypoechoic tendon with cortical irregularity at the lateral facet of the greater trochanter. Which tendon is most likely involved?
exam2.explanation: The gluteus medius inserts on the lateral and superoposterior facets of the greater trochanter, and its tendinopathy is the most common source of greater trochanteric pain syndrome. The gluteus minimus inserts on the anterior facet.
exam2.hint: Map each trochanteric facet to the tendon that inserts on it.

exam2.question: A 58-year-old woman with obesity reports progressive flattening of the right arch and medial ankle pain; she cannot do a single-leg heel rise. Sonography shows a thickened, heterogeneous tendon posterior to the medial malleolus with sheath fluid and a longitudinal split near the navicular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Degeneration and tearing of the posterior tibial tendon is the leading cause of adult acquired flatfoot, classically in middle-aged women, with an inability to perform a single-leg heel rise. The posterior tibial tendon is the most anterior tendon behind the medial malleolus.
exam2.hint: Consider which medial ankle tendon failure leads to collapse of the arch.

exam2.question: A 46-year-old man felt a sudden pop in the mid calf while lunging for a tennis ball. Sonography shows disruption of the distal medial gastrocnemius at its junction with the aponeurosis and a fluid collection between the medial gastrocnemius and the soleus. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Plantaris tendon rupture without muscle injury
Tennis leg from medial gastrocnemius myotendinous tear

exam2.explanation: Tennis leg is a tear of the distal medial head of the gastrocnemius at the musculotendinous junction, often with fluid between gastrocnemius and soleus. A ruptured Baker cyst tracks from the knee and lacks muscle fiber disruption.
exam2.hint: The tear is at the distal end of the medial head, where it meets the aponeurosis.

exam2.question: During carpal tunnel sonography in a 39-year-old woman, the median nerve is divided into two separate fascicle bundles with a small artery between them that shows pulsatile flow on color Doppler. How should median nerve size be assessed?

options.text: Exclude the patient from CSA measurement because the variant is uninterpretable
Add the CSAs of both nerve bundles and compare the sum with normal values
Measure the area of the persistent median artery

exam2.explanation: A bifid median nerve with a persistent median artery is a normal variant, and the CSAs of both bundles should be summed for comparison with standard thresholds. Measuring only one bundle underestimates nerve size.
exam2.hint: Consider whether a bifid nerve should be judged by part of its fibers or all of them.

exam2.question: While scanning the volar wrist of a 44-year-old woman, a student is unsure which structure is the median nerve among the flexor tendons. Which observation best identifies the nerve?

options.text: It becomes markedly hypoechoic with slight transducer tilting
It glides several centimeters with finger flexion
It shows bright fibrillar echoes in short axis
It shows less change in echogenicity with transducer tilting and moves less than the tendons with finger flexion

exam2.explanation: Tendons are highly anisotropic and glide with finger motion, whereas the median nerve has a fascicular pattern, is less anisotropic, and moves little. Marked darkening with slight tilting is characteristic of tendons.
exam2.hint: Compare how much each structure depends on beam angle and on finger movement.

exam2.question: A 79-year-old woman has an acute hot, swollen knee. Sonography shows thin hyperechoic linear deposits within the middle layer of the femoral hyaline cartilage, parallel to the bone surface, and punctate echogenic foci within the menisci. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: CPPD deposits appear within the substance of hyaline cartilage and fibrocartilage such as the menisci, whereas gout's urate layer lies on the cartilage surface. Osteophytes arise at bone margins, not within cartilage.
exam2.hint: Locate the crystals relative to the cartilage: on its surface or within it.

exam2.question: During a dynamic exam of a 44-year-old painter with painful arc, the patient abducts the arm while the transducer sits in the coronal plane at the lateral acromion. Which finding is the sonographic sign of subacromial impingement?

options.text: Anterior subluxation of the biceps tendon from the groove during external rotation
Widening of the acromioclavicular joint during downward arm traction
Bunching and pooling of the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa against the acromion as the greater tuberosity passes beneath it
Posterior translation of the humeral head during internal rotation

exam2.explanation: In subacromial impingement, the bursa and cuff bunch up lateral to the acromion and fail to glide smoothly beneath it during abduction, often reproducing pain. Biceps subluxation is assessed with external rotation and is a separate dynamic test.
exam2.hint: Focus on what should glide smoothly under the coracoacromial arch during abduction.

exam2.question: A 61-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis has sudden calf pain and swelling. Compression sonography shows fully compressible deep veins. A thin fluid collection with a pointed inferior margin tracks from the posteromedial knee down along the superficial surface of the medial gastrocnemius. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tennis leg from medial gastrocnemius tear
Deep venous thrombosis of the gastrocnemius veins

exam2.explanation: Leakage of a Baker cyst produces fluid dissecting inferiorly into the calf with a tapered margin, mimicking DVT clinically (pseudothrombophlebitis). Tennis leg shows a tear at the medial gastrocnemius musculotendinous junction with fluid between gastrocnemius and soleus.
exam2.hint: Track the fluid back to its source near the knee joint in a patient with arthritis.

exam2.question: A 55-year-old man had a below-knee amputation two years ago and now has sharp pain at one point on the stump that limits prosthesis use. Sonography shows a focal hypoechoic fusiform mass at the end of a transected nerve, continuous with it, and pressing the transducer over it reproduces his pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: After transection, disorganized axonal regrowth forms a bulbous terminal neuroma at the nerve end, and sonopalpation reproducing pain supports it as the pain generator. A neuroma in continuity occurs in a nerve that remains intact.
exam2.hint: The nerve was cut, so the swelling sits at its end rather than along an intact course.

exam2.question: While evaluating a suspected rotator cuff tear in a 57-year-old man, the sonographer looks for indirect signs. Which secondary finding most supports a full-thickness supraspinatus tear?

options.text: Concave sagging of the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa contour over the defect
Convex bulging of the bursa above an intact tendon
Uniform tendon thickening with preserved fibrillar pattern
Clean posterior shadowing from an intratendinous focus

exam2.explanation: Loss of the normal convex outer cuff contour, with the bursa and deltoid sagging into the defect, is a recognized secondary sign of full-thickness tear, along with the cartilage interface sign and cortical irregularity. A convex bursa over an intact tendon is the normal contour.
exam2.hint: Think about what happens to the overlying soft tissues when tendon volume is lost.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old soldier has a painless bump on the anterior lower leg that becomes more prominent when standing and during exertion. Sonography shows a focal defect in the overlying fascia through which the tibialis anterior bulges during active dorsiflexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A muscle hernia is muscle protruding through a fascial defect, typically in the tibialis anterior, and is best shown dynamically with contraction. A lipoma would be a fat-containing mass without a fascial defect.
exam2.hint: The finding appears or worsens with muscle contraction.

exam2.question: A 45-year-old carpet installer has a soft swelling over the front of the knee. Sonography shows a compressible anechoic collection directly superficial to the patella, with no connection to the joint. Which bursa is involved?
exam2.explanation: Repetitive kneeling distends the prepatellar bursa, which lies superficial to the patella and does not communicate with the joint. The suprapatellar bursa is a joint recess deep to the quadriceps tendon.
exam2.hint: The collection lies superficial to a bone, not deep to a tendon.

exam2.question: A sonographer compares the anterior hip recesses in a child with a unilateral limp, measuring from the anterior femoral neck cortex to the outer joint capsule. Which finding most supports a joint effusion on the symptomatic side?

options.text: A concave capsule paralleling the femoral neck
A hyperechoic capsule thinner than the contralateral side
A convex, distended capsule with a difference of more than 2 mm from the asymptomatic side

exam2.explanation: An effusion bulges the anterior capsule convexly away from the femoral neck, and an asymmetry greater than about 2 mm compared with the normal side is a widely used criterion. A concave capsule paralleling the neck is the normal appearance.
exam2.hint: Recall the normal shape of the anterior hip capsule and how much asymmetry is accepted.

exam2.question: A 16-year-old girl felt her kneecap shift out of place during a cutting maneuver, and it spontaneously reduced. Sonography shows a large effusion and thickening with discontinuity of a ligament at the medial margin of the patella. Which ligament is most likely torn?
exam2.explanation: Transient lateral patellar dislocation commonly tears the medial patellofemoral ligament, the primary restraint against lateral patellar translation. The lateral retinaculum is not stretched by a lateral dislocation.
exam2.hint: The patella dislocates laterally, so the restraint on the opposite side fails.

exam2.question: A 50-year-old man felt a pop in the antecubital fossa while lifting furniture. The distal biceps tendon is absent from the radial tuberosity, yet the tendon stump has retracted only about 2 cm. Which structure most likely limits retraction?
exam2.explanation: When the lacertus fibrosus remains intact it tethers the biceps to the forearm fascia and limits proximal retraction, which can make a complete tear clinically subtle. The brachialis inserts on the ulna and does not tether the biceps tendon.
exam2.hint: Think about which part of the distal biceps tendon complex does not insert on the radius.

exam2.question: A 22-year-old football player had an external rotation injury to the ankle and has pain above the ankle joint anteriorly. Sonography shows a thickened, discontinuous anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, with widening of the tibiofibular gap during external rotation stress. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: External rotation injuries tear the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament of the syndesmosis, and dynamic widening of the tibiofibular gap supports instability. The anterior talofibular ligament runs from the fibula to the talus at the joint level, not between tibia and fibula.
exam2.hint: Note which bones the injured ligament connects and the mechanism of injury.

exam2.question: A sonographer uses a posterior approach to image the distal biceps tendon insertion on the radial tuberosity in a 47-year-old patient. Which forearm position best brings the insertion into view from the dorsal side?

options.text: Neutral rotation with the wrist flexed

exam2.explanation: Pronation rotates the radial tuberosity posteriorly, so the biceps insertion can be seen from a dorsal approach between the radius and ulna. Supination turns the tuberosity anteriorly and is used for the anterior approach.
exam2.hint: Picture which way the radial tuberosity rotates as the forearm turns palm-down.

exam2.question: A 40-year-old violinist has weakness of finger and thumb extension without sensory loss; wrist extension is preserved but deviates radially. Sonography shows a swollen, hypoechoic nerve just proximal to the supinator muscle. Which diagnosis best fits?

options.text: Radial nerve compression in the spiral groove
Posterior interosseous nerve compression at the arcade of Frohse
Superficial radial nerve entrapment at the wrist
Ulnar nerve compression in Guyon canal

exam2.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve is a purely motor branch that enters the supinator under the arcade of Frohse; compression produces finger drop with radial deviation of the wrist and no sensory deficit. Spiral groove compression affects the radial nerve proximally, causing wrist drop and sensory loss.
exam2.hint: Use the pattern of preserved and lost function, and the absence of sensory loss, to localize the lesion along the radial nerve.

exam2.question: When evaluating hyperemia in rheumatoid wrist synovitis with power Doppler, which technical error would most likely cause a false-negative result?

options.text: Setting the pulse repetition frequency low
Pressing firmly with the transducer on the dorsal wrist
Setting Doppler gain just below the noise threshold

exam2.explanation: Excess transducer pressure compresses small synovial vessels and can abolish their low-velocity flow; a light touch with plenty of gel is recommended. Low PRF, low wall filter, and gain just below noise are the correct settings for detecting slow flow.
exam2.hint: Three of the options describe settings that favor slow-flow detection; find the one that works against it.

exam2.question: A 49-year-old woman has painful overhead activity. Long-axis imaging of the supraspinatus shows a focal anechoic defect at the footprint that involves the deep fibers adjacent to the humeral head and does not reach the bursal surface; the bursal contour is preserved. Which diagnosis best fits?
exam2.explanation: A defect that reaches the articular (deep) surface but spares the bursal surface is an articular-sided partial-thickness tear, the most common partial tear type. A full-thickness tear would extend from the articular to the bursal surface.
exam2.hint: Note which surface the defect touches and which surface it spares.
keywords: does not reach the bursal surface

exam2.question: A 26-year-old baseball pitcher has vague posterior shoulder pain. Sonography shows fatty, hyperechoic atrophy isolated to the teres minor with normal rotator cuff tendons. Compression of which nerve is most likely?

options.text: Axillary nerve in the quadrilateral space
Suprascapular nerve at the spinoglenoid notch
Long thoracic nerve along the chest wall

exam2.explanation: The axillary nerve passes through the quadrilateral space and innervates the teres minor and deltoid, so quadrilateral space syndrome produces isolated teres minor atrophy. Suprascapular nerve compression affects the infraspinatus with or without the supraspinatus.
exam2.hint: Match the atrophied muscle to its motor nerve and that nerve's anatomic tunnel.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old rugby player has a thigh hematoma scanned one hour after a collision; it appears ill-defined and echogenic. If it is scanned again over the next one to two weeks, which evolution is most expected?

options.text: It becomes more hypoechoic to anechoic and better defined as the clot liquefies
It becomes increasingly hyperechoic with dense posterior shadowing
It converts to a solid mass with internal arterial flow

exam2.explanation: Acute hematomas are often echogenic, then become hypoechoic or anechoic with septations and fluid levels as clot lyses, before organizing and shrinking. Internal arterial flow would raise concern for a hemorrhagic tumor rather than simple hematoma.
exam2.hint: Think about what happens to clot over days.

exam2.question: A 68-year-old man on long-term hemodialysis stumbled and now cannot actively extend his knee. Sonography above the patella shows a fluid-filled gap with wavy retracted tendon fibers, and the patella lies lower than on the other side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Quadriceps tendon rupture typically affects older patients with systemic risk factors such as renal failure, diabetes, or steroid use, and the patella drops to a low position. Patellar tendon rupture produces a high-riding patella and occurs more often in younger patients.
exam2.hint: Use the location of the gap and the direction of patellar displacement.

exam2.question: A 27-year-old basketball player felt a pop while landing a jump and cannot perform a straight-leg raise. Sonography shows discontinuity of the tendon just below the inferior pole of the patella, and the patella sits higher than on the other side. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Disruption below the inferior pole with a high-riding patella (patella alta) indicates patellar tendon rupture, typical of younger athletes. Quadriceps tendon rupture lies above the patella and causes a low-lying patella.
exam2.hint: A high-riding patella means its inferior restraint has failed.

exam2.question: For an interscalene brachial plexus evaluation, in which location are the C5 to C7 roots typically seen as a vertical row of round hypoechoic structures?

options.text: Anterior to the anterior scalene muscle
Medial to the common carotid artery
Between the anterior and middle scalene muscles

exam2.explanation: In the interscalene groove the upper roots appear as stacked round hypoechoic structures between the anterior and middle scalenes, often called the traffic light appearance. The phrenic nerve, not the plexus, runs on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene.
exam2.hint: Recall the traffic light appearance and the muscles on either side of it.

exam2.question: A 64-year-old man cannot actively abduct his arm after a fall on the outstretched hand. Sonography shows no visible supraspinatus between the deltoid and the humeral head, with the deltoid lying directly on the humeral head cartilage and an irregular greater tuberosity cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Resorptive-phase calcific tendinopathy of the supraspinatus
Massive full-thickness supraspinatus tear with retraction
Adhesive capsulitis with rotator interval thickening

exam2.explanation: Nonvisualization of the cuff with the deltoid contacting the humeral head is the most specific sign of a large full-thickness tear with retraction. A bursal-sided partial tear leaves articular-side fibers covering the humeral head.
exam2.hint: Ask what normally separates the deltoid from the humeral head cartilage and what it means when nothing does.

exam2.question: A 19-year-old football player had a thigh contusion five weeks ago and now has a firm, enlarging, tender mass. Sonography shows a mass in the vastus intermedius with a peripheral rim of echogenic calcification casting posterior shadowing and a hypoechoic center. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Myositis ossificans matures from the periphery inward, producing a zonal pattern with peripheral calcification several weeks after trauma, which sonography can detect before radiographs. Osteosarcoma typically mineralizes centrally and lacks the zonal pattern.
exam2.hint: The direction of mineralization helps separate a benign posttraumatic process from a malignant one.

exam2.question: Several weeks after a corticosteroid injection for De Quervain tenosynovitis, a 40-year-old woman notices a depressed, lighter-colored area of skin at the injection site. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Tendon rupture of the abductor pollicis longus
Subcutaneous fat atrophy and skin depigmentation from superficial steroid deposition

exam2.explanation: Steroid deposited in the subcutaneous fat rather than the tendon sheath can cause fat atrophy and depigmentation, especially in darker skin; accurate sheath placement under ultrasound reduces this risk. Tendon rupture would cause loss of function rather than skin changes.
exam2.hint: Consider what can happen when steroid is deposited outside the intended target.

exam2.question: For an anterior ultrasound-guided hip aspiration, which target and safety step are most appropriate?

options.text: Target the greater trochanter and avoid the sciatic nerve
Target the acetabular labrum and avoid the obturator artery
Target the iliopsoas muscle belly and avoid the inguinal ligament
Target the anterior recess at the femoral head-neck junction and identify the femoral vessels with color Doppler first

exam2.explanation: The anterior synovial recess at the femoral head-neck junction is the usual target, and the femoral neurovascular bundle lies medially, so Doppler mapping before needle entry improves safety. The greater trochanter is extra-articular.
exam2.hint: Locate where hip joint fluid collects anteriorly and what lies medial to it.

exam2.question: A 66-year-old man with hyperuricemia has an afebrile, swollen posterior elbow. The olecranon bursa is distended with hypoechoic fluid containing clustered hyperechoic aggregates that do not shadow, plus peripheral hyperemia. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Rheumatoid nodule within the olecranon bursa
Chronic traumatic bursitis with organized hematoma
Gouty olecranon bursitis with tophaceous material
Synovial osteochondromatosis of the elbow joint

exam2.explanation: Hyperechoic aggregates within a distended bursa in a hyperuricemic patient suggest tophaceous gout, which commonly involves the olecranon bursa. Organized hematoma is possible after trauma but does not explain the hyperuricemia and aggregates.
exam2.hint: Consider the echotexture of the material in the bursa and whether it shadows.

exam2.question: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has months of progressive shoulder pain with marked loss of passive external rotation. The rotator cuff is intact. The coracohumeral ligament is thickened in the rotator interval, with hypoechoic soft tissue and increased Doppler flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Thickening of the coracohumeral ligament and hyperemic soft tissue in the rotator interval, together with loss of passive external rotation in a diabetic patient, are typical of adhesive capsulitis. Osteoarthritis would show osteophytes and cartilage loss, which these findings do not include.
exam2.hint: Weigh the loss of passive motion and the location of the soft tissue abnormality.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old ice hockey player has chronic exertional groin pain without a palpable bulge. Sonography shows a hypoechoic cleft at the pubic attachment of the common rectus abdominis-adductor longus aponeurosis, and no hernia sac is seen with Valsalva. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Athletic pubalgia, the so-called sports hernia, involves injury to the rectus abdominis-adductor longus aponeurotic plate at the pubis rather than a true hernia. A direct inguinal hernia would show a sac protruding through the posterior inguinal wall with Valsalva.
exam2.hint: The term sports hernia is a misnomer; focus on the injured aponeurosis.

exam2.question: A 72-year-old man treated for pneumonia two weeks ago now has bilateral posterior ankle pain, and sonography shows a partial Achilles tear. Which medication history is most relevant?
exam2.explanation: Fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin increase the risk of Achilles tendinopathy and rupture, especially in older adults and those using corticosteroids. Macrolides used for pneumonia do not carry this tendon warning.
exam2.hint: Consider which drug class prescribed for pneumonia is linked to tendon injury in older adults.

exam2.question: A sonographer needs to evaluate a digital flexor tendon pulley and the volar plate of a small finger joint. Which approach provides the best resolution?

options.text: Low-frequency curvilinear transducer with harmonic imaging
Phased-array transducer with a wide sector
Standard linear transducer at its lowest frequency setting
High-frequency compact linear (hockey-stick) transducer with a thick layer of gel

exam2.explanation: Small, superficial finger structures are best seen with a high-frequency small-footprint linear transducer, and generous gel acts as a standoff to place them in the focal region. Low-frequency transducers sacrifice the resolution needed for millimeter structures.
exam2.hint: Superficial millimeter-sized targets need both high frequency and good contact.

exam2.question: Why is power Doppler often preferred over color Doppler for detecting inflammatory hyperemia in tendons and synovium?

options.text: It displays flow direction more clearly
It provides accurate peak velocity measurements
It is more sensitive to low-velocity flow and less angle dependent

exam2.explanation: Power Doppler encodes the amplitude of the Doppler signal, making it more sensitive to slow flow in small vessels and less angle dependent, though it does not show direction. It remains susceptible to motion (flash) artifact.
exam2.hint: Consider what power Doppler encodes and what it gives up.

exam2.question: A 6-week-old girl born breech undergoes hip sonography. On the standard coronal view the alpha angle measures 54 degrees and the femoral head is centered. How is this hip classified by the Graf method?

options.text: Type I, a mature normal hip
Type IIa, a physiologically immature hip that needs follow-up

exam2.explanation: In the Graf method an alpha angle of 60 degrees or more is type I, while 50 to 59 degrees in an infant younger than 3 months is type IIa (physiologically immature) and warrants follow-up. Types III and IV are decentered or dislocated, which a centered femoral head excludes.
exam2.hint: Compare the angle with the 60-degree normal threshold and factor in the infant's age.

exam2.question: A surgeon is deciding between operative and functional nonoperative treatment for an acute complete Achilles rupture in a 52-year-old man. Which dynamic sonographic assessment is most useful?

options.text: Measuring tendon thickness with the ankle in full dorsiflexion
Applying color Doppler to the paratenon
Observing whether the tendon ends appose with gentle passive plantar flexion
Comparing the calcaneal cortex with the opposite side

exam2.explanation: Passive plantar flexion shows whether the torn ends come into contact; apposition supports nonoperative treatment in a plantarflexed boot, while a persistent gap favors surgery. Forced dorsiflexion risks widening the gap and does not answer the management question.
exam2.hint: Ask which ankle position answers whether the tendon ends can heal in contact.

exam2.question: A sonographer needs to expose the anterior supraspinatus footprint from beneath the acromion in a 55-year-old patient who can tolerate positioning. Which arm position is preferred?

options.text: Modified Crass position with the palm on the back pocket and the elbow directed posteriorly
Arm at the side with the elbow flexed and the palm facing up
Arm in full external rotation with the elbow against the side
Hand placed on the opposite shoulder across the chest

exam2.explanation: The modified Crass position extends and internally rotates the shoulder, bringing the supraspinatus out from under the acromion while keeping it less tense than the original Crass position. The neutral palm-up position is used for the biceps groove, and external rotation for the subscapularis.
exam2.hint: Think about the motion that rotates the greater tuberosity anteriorly out from under the acromion.

exam2.question: A 35-year-old man fell from a motorcycle and slid along the road. Two weeks later he has a fluctuant swelling over the lateral hip. Sonography shows a large hypoechoic fluid collection with floating echogenic fat lobules lying between the subcutaneous fat and the fascia lata. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Gluteus medius tendon tear with hematoma

exam2.explanation: A shearing injury that separates the subcutaneous tissue from the underlying fascia, creating a collection containing fat lobules over the greater trochanter, is a Morel-Lavallee lesion. Trochanteric bursitis lies deep to the iliotibial band and gluteus maximus rather than superficial to the fascia.
exam2.hint: Locate the collection relative to the fascia lata and remember the shearing mechanism.

exam2.question: During an out-of-plane needle approach for a small ganglion aspiration, the sonographer sees an echogenic dot in the target. What is the main pitfall of relying on this dot?

options.text: The dot represents reverberation from the transducer and not the needle
The dot may represent the needle shaft rather than the tip, so the tip could be deeper than appreciated
The dot always indicates that the needle has bent
The dot indicates that the needle has passed through the target

exam2.explanation: In out-of-plane technique the beam crosses the needle as an echogenic dot, which may be any part of the shaft; the tip can lie deeper unless it is tracked with a walk-down technique or small jiggling movements. In-plane technique shows the entire shaft and tip.
exam2.hint: Think about which part of the needle the beam is crossing in an out-of-plane view.

exam2.question: A 50-year-old runner has chronic medial heel pain unresponsive to treatment for plantar fasciitis. The plantar fascia measures 3.5 mm, while the abductor digiti minimi muscle is small and hyperechoic compared with the other foot. Entrapment of which nerve is most likely?
exam2.explanation: The inferior calcaneal nerve, the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve, supplies the abductor digiti minimi, so its entrapment causes heel pain and fatty atrophy of that muscle. A normal fascia thickness points away from plantar fasciitis.
exam2.hint: Identify the nerve that supplies the atrophied muscle and passes near the heel.
