exam2.question: In short axis, the long head biceps tendon in its groove appears hypoechoic and could be mistaken for fluid. Which maneuver best corrects this artifact?

options.text: Rotate the transducer 90 degrees and measure in long axis only
Toggle the transducer cranially or caudally to make the beam perpendicular to the tendon
Increase the depth to include the humeral head
Turn on spatial compound imaging and increase pressure

exam2.explanation: Because the tendon runs obliquely in the groove, tilting (toggling) the transducer in short axis aligns the beam perpendicular to the fibers and restores their echogenicity. Long-axis imaging alone does not resolve a short-axis anisotropy question.
exam2.hint: Consider why a tendon running obliquely can look dark in short axis.

exam2.question: A 47-year-old man has a firm lump along the lateral joint line of the knee. Sonography shows a multilocular anechoic cyst adjacent to the meniscus with a hypoechoic linear cleft extending from the cyst into the meniscus. Which meniscal abnormality is most often associated?

options.text: Radial tear of the meniscal root

exam2.explanation: Parameniscal cysts form when joint fluid is pumped through a meniscal tear, most often a horizontal cleavage tear, into the adjacent soft tissue. Treating the cyst without addressing the tear tends to result in recurrence.
exam2.hint: The cleft connecting the cyst to the meniscus shows the pathway for the fluid.

exam2.question: To maximize detection of a small knee effusion in the suprapatellar recess, how should the knee be positioned?

options.text: Flexed 90 degrees with the foot flat
Hyperextended with the patella pushed distally
Flexed about 20 to 30 degrees with the quadriceps contracted

exam2.explanation: Slight flexion with quadriceps contraction displaces fluid from the posterior and lateral recesses into the suprapatellar recess, making small effusions easier to see. Deep flexion compresses the suprapatellar recess and displaces fluid elsewhere.
exam2.hint: Consider which position pushes fluid into the anterior superior recess rather than away from it.

exam2.question: A 45-year-old man felt a kick in the back of the calf while playing tennis and has a positive Thompson test. Sonography shows a 4 cm gap in the Achilles tendon about 5 cm above the calcaneus, filled with hematoma, but a thin intact tendon remains along the medial side of the gap. What does this intact band most likely represent?

options.text: Residual intact Achilles fibers indicating a partial tear

exam2.explanation: The plantaris tendon runs along the medial Achilles and is often spared in Achilles ruptures, so it can be mistaken for residual Achilles fibers and can mask a complete tear clinically. The flexor hallucis longus lies deeper, anterior to Kager fat pad.
exam2.hint: Recall which structures run alongside the Achilles and where each lies.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old distance runner has lateral knee pain that begins after a few kilometers. Sonography shows hypoechoic edema and a small fluid collection deep to the iliotibial band at the lateral femoral epicondyle, with a normal-thickness band distally. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Repetitive friction of the iliotibial band over the lateral femoral epicondyle in runners produces edema or fluid deep to the band at that level. A lateral meniscal cyst would sit at the joint line, connected to the meniscus.
exam2.hint: Correlate the location at the epicondyle with a repetitive-motion sport.

exam2.question: A 7-year-old boy refuses to bear weight on the right leg. His temperature is 39.2 C, WBC is 15,000/uL, and ESR is 55 mm/h. Sonography shows a distended anterior recess of the right hip with anechoic fluid. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat sonography in one week to document resolution
Urgent ultrasound-guided aspiration of the hip joint
Discharge with anti-inflammatory medication for transient synovitis
Compression ultrasound of the femoral vein

exam2.explanation: Fever, inability to bear weight, elevated WBC, and elevated ESR meet multiple Kocher criteria for septic arthritis, so the effusion must be aspirated urgently. Transient synovitis is a diagnosis of exclusion and cannot be assumed from anechoic fluid.
exam2.hint: Count how many clinical prediction criteria for joint infection this child meets.

exam2.question: A 34-year-old man had an anterior shoulder dislocation two weeks ago. Short-axis imaging shows an empty bicipital groove, with the long head biceps tendon lying medially over the lesser tuberosity. Which associated injury is most likely?
exam2.explanation: Medial dislocation of the long head biceps tendon requires disruption of the medial stabilizers of the groove, typically the subscapularis tendon and the biceps pulley. Infraspinatus tears are posterior and do not allow medial biceps displacement.
exam2.hint: Consider which tendon forms the medial wall of support for the biceps as it leaves the groove.

exam2.question: A 70-year-old man with recurrent painful knee attacks has a serum urate of 9.6 mg/dL. Sonography of the femoral trochlea shows an irregular hyperechoic band on the surface of the anechoic hyaline cartilage that remains visible regardless of insonation angle. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Gout, demonstrated by the double contour sign
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition within the cartilage

exam2.explanation: Monosodium urate deposited on the surface of hyaline cartilage creates the double contour sign, which persists at all insonation angles. Calcium pyrophosphate deposits lie within the middle layer of the cartilage rather than on its surface, and the normal interface line disappears when the beam is not perpendicular.
exam2.hint: Note whether the crystal layer sits on the cartilage surface or inside it.

exam2.question: A 47-year-old woman has carpal tunnel syndrome. In long axis, how does the median nerve typically appear at the proximal edge of the flexor retinaculum?

options.text: Uniform caliber with a preserved fascicular pattern throughout
Fusiform swelling distal to the retinaculum with normal caliber proximally
Anechoic tubular dilation with posterior acoustic enhancement
Hypoechoic swelling proximal to the tunnel with abrupt narrowing beneath the retinaculum (notch sign)

exam2.explanation: In carpal tunnel syndrome the median nerve swells and loses its fascicular pattern proximal to the tunnel, then narrows abruptly where the flexor retinaculum compresses it, producing the notch sign in long axis. Swelling forms proximal to the compression, not distal to it.
exam2.hint: Picture the nerve contour on either side of the point of compression.

exam2.question: During an ultrasound-guided subacromial bursal injection, the needle tip lies within the supraspinatus tendon and injection meets high resistance. What should be done next?

options.text: Withdraw slightly until the tip lies in the bursa, where injectate flows freely and distends it
Advance the needle deeper into the glenohumeral joint
Inject half the dose into the tendon and the rest into the deltoid

exam2.explanation: Injecting corticosteroid into tendon substance risks tendon damage, and high resistance suggests intratendinous placement; the tip should be repositioned until fluid is seen distending the bursa. Forceful injection into the tendon is harmful.
exam2.hint: Watch for the target space distending freely in real time.

exam2.question: A 64-year-old woman with diabetes and obesity has pain at the anteromedial proximal tibia about 5 cm below the joint line. Sonography shows a fluid collection deep to the converging tendons that insert there. Which tendons form this insertion?
exam2.explanation: The pes anserinus is formed by the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus tendons inserting on the anteromedial proximal tibia, and pes anserine bursitis lies deep to them. The semimembranosus inserts more posteromedially and is not part of the pes.
exam2.hint: Recall the three tendons that insert on the anteromedial proximal tibia and which hamstring is not among them.

exam2.question: An 8-year-old boy has a red, painful sole of the foot three days after stepping on a wooden deck; radiographs are negative. Sonography shows a 6 mm linear hyperechoic focus with posterior shadowing surrounded by a hypoechoic rim. What does the hypoechoic rim most likely represent?

options.text: Inflammatory reaction with edema or granulation tissue
Air trapped along the puncture tract

exam2.explanation: A hypoechoic halo around a foreign body develops within a day or two from inflammation, edema, or granulation tissue and makes the object easier to find. Wood is radiolucent, which is why sonography is valuable here.
exam2.hint: Consider the body's response to an organic object left in the tissue for several days.

exam2.question: A 71-year-old woman has bilateral masses at the inferior tips of the scapulae that become apparent with arm flexion. Sonography shows poorly marginated masses deep to the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi, with alternating curvilinear echogenic and hypoechoic layers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Elastofibroma dorsi occurs in older adults beneath the scapular tip, often bilaterally, with a layered pattern of fibroelastic and fatty tissue. Liposarcoma is not typically bilateral at this characteristic location.
exam2.hint: Bilateral involvement at a specific periscapular location is strongly diagnostic.

exam2.question: A 23-year-old soccer player has a complete anterior talofibular ligament tear after a severe inversion injury. Which ligament is the next most commonly injured and should be evaluated deep to the peroneal tendons?
exam2.explanation: Lateral ankle sprains progress from the anterior talofibular ligament to the calcaneofibular ligament, which lies deep to the peroneal tendons and is best seen with dorsiflexion. The posterior talofibular ligament is rarely injured.
exam2.hint: Lateral ligament injuries follow a predictable anterior-to-posterior sequence.

exam2.question: A 55-year-old woman has a soft, painless, slowly growing mass on her upper back. Sonography shows a compressible, oval, well-circumscribed mass in the subcutaneous fat whose long axis is parallel to the skin, isoechoic to fat with thin echogenic striations, and no internal Doppler flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A compressible, oval mass parallel to the skin, isoechoic to fat with thin echogenic lines and minimal or no flow, is classic for subcutaneous lipoma. An epidermal inclusion cyst is hypoechoic with internal echoes, posterior enhancement, and often a tract to the skin.
exam2.hint: Compare the echotexture of the mass with the surrounding fat.

exam2.question: A 38-year-old man has a reducible groin bulge. During Valsalva, a hernia sac containing fat emerges from the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and travels along the inguinal canal. What type of hernia is this?
exam2.explanation: Indirect inguinal hernias arise from the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and follow the canal, while direct hernias protrude medial to the vessels through Hesselbach triangle. Femoral hernias lie below the inguinal ligament.
exam2.hint: Use the inferior epigastric vessels as the dividing landmark.

exam2.question: A 40-year-old man had a medial knee injury two years ago. Sonography shows a linear echogenic focus with posterior shadowing along the proximal medial collateral ligament near the medial femoral condyle. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Acute avulsion fracture of the adductor tubercle
Pellegrini-Stieda ossification from a prior MCL injury

exam2.explanation: Posttraumatic calcification or ossification along the proximal MCL after an old injury is the Pellegrini-Stieda lesion. An acute avulsion would accompany a recent injury with hematoma rather than a remote history.
exam2.hint: Consider the time since injury and the ligament the calcification lies within.

exam2.question: A 29-year-old woman has a firm dorsal wrist bump that enlarges with activity. Sonography shows an anechoic, multilocular, noncompressible cyst with posterior enhancement and a thin neck extending deep toward the carpal bones. From which structure does it most often arise?

options.text: Extensor carpi radialis brevis tendon sheath
Lunotriquetral ligament on the volar side

exam2.explanation: Most dorsal wrist ganglia arise from the dorsal scapholunate ligament, and tracing the neck to its origin aids surgical planning. Volar ganglia more often arise from the radioscaphoid or scaphotrapezial joints.
exam2.hint: Follow the neck of the cyst to its point of origin.

exam2.question: A 74-year-old man has a pulsatile mass behind the knee. Sonography shows a fusiform dilation of the popliteal artery measuring 2.2 cm with mural thrombus. Which associated finding should be evaluated next?

options.text: Tibial nerve enlargement at the tarsal tunnel
Contralateral popliteal and abdominal aortic aneurysms

exam2.explanation: Popliteal artery aneurysms are frequently bilateral and commonly coexist with abdominal aortic aneurysms, so both should be screened. A Baker cyst would show a neck to the gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa and no arterial flow.
exam2.hint: Consider which associated conditions change management of a popliteal artery aneurysm.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old tennis player has painful snapping at the dorsal ulnar wrist. Dynamic imaging during forearm supination with wrist flexion shows the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon displacing out of its groove onto the ulnar side of the distal ulna. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ulnar nerve dislocation in Guyon canal
Extensor carpi ulnaris instability from subsheath injury

exam2.explanation: Supination with flexion provokes extensor carpi ulnaris subluxation when its fibro-osseous subsheath is torn, a recognized injury in racquet sports. A TFCC perforation does not cause a visible tendon to leave its groove.
exam2.hint: The snapping structure is a tendon leaving its groove, so think about what normally holds it there.

exam2.question: A 72-year-old woman has a small tender lump in the upper medial thigh just below the inguinal ligament. During Valsalva, a sac containing fat protrudes medial to the common femoral vein, which is compressed by it. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Femoral hernias pass below the inguinal ligament through the femoral canal medial to the femoral vein and are most common in older women. A saphena varix is a dilated venous structure with venous flow at the saphenofemoral junction, not a fat-containing sac.
exam2.hint: The relationship to the inguinal ligament and femoral vein defines the canal involved.

exam2.question: A 58-year-old man has anterior shoulder pain. Fluid surrounds the long head biceps tendon in the bicipital groove. Which finding most supports primary biceps tenosynovitis rather than glenohumeral joint fluid tracking into the sheath?

options.text: Thin anechoic fluid symmetrically surrounding a tendon of normal caliber
Sheath fluid disproportionate to joint fluid, with synovial thickening and Doppler hyperemia of the sheath
Fluid in the posterior glenohumeral recess

exam2.explanation: Because the biceps sheath communicates with the glenohumeral joint, a small amount of sheath fluid commonly reflects a joint effusion. Fluid out of proportion to the joint, with synovial thickening and hyperemia of the sheath, favors primary tenosynovitis. Posterior recess fluid indicates a joint effusion, and bursal fluid lies outside the sheath.
exam2.hint: Consider the sheath's relationship to the joint and what would make the sheath itself the primary source.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old has a painful palm after a broken bottle injury. Sonography shows a bright linear focus in the subcutaneous tissue. Which artifact behind the focus most supports glass or metal rather than wood?
exam2.explanation: Glass and metal commonly produce reverberation or comet-tail artifact because of strong acoustic impedance mismatches with smooth surfaces, while wood typically produces clean shadowing. Posterior enhancement occurs behind fluid.
exam2.hint: Compare how the surfaces of glass or metal and of wood interact with the beam.

exam2.question: A 24-year-old runner has a visible lateral hip snap during flexion and extension while lying on the opposite side. Dynamic sonography over the greater trochanter shows a band of tissue catching and then abruptly moving over the trochanter. Which structure is most likely responsible?

options.text: Iliotibial band or anterior edge of the gluteus maximus

exam2.explanation: External snapping hip results from the posterior iliotibial band or anterior gluteus maximus catching on the greater trochanter during hip flexion-extension. The iliopsoas causes internal snapping in the anterior groin.
exam2.hint: Consider which structures pass over the greater trochanter during hip flexion and extension.

exam2.question: During a perineural injection for carpal tunnel syndrome, fluid is injected under ultrasound guidance to separate the median nerve from the flexor retinaculum and surrounding tissues. What is this technique called?
exam2.explanation: Hydrodissection uses fluid injected around a nerve to separate it from adjacent tissue, freeing adhesions and creating a safe path for the needle. Barbotage is lavage of calcific deposits.
exam2.hint: Barbotage, tenotomy, and arthrography each have a different target; which technique targets the space around a nerve?

exam2.question: A 32-year-old woman with a cam-type femoroacetabular morphology has anterior groin pain and clicking. Sonography of the anterior hip shows a hypoechoic cleft at the base of the anterosuperior labrum and an adjacent lobulated anechoic cyst. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Acetabular labral tear with paralabral cyst
Ganglion of the rectus femoris tendon
Synovial herniation pit of the femoral neck

exam2.explanation: A hypoechoic cleft at the labral base with an adjacent paralabral cyst indicates a labral tear, often associated with femoroacetabular impingement. Iliopsoas bursitis would be a larger collection along the iliopsoas tendon without a labral defect.
exam2.hint: Consider how a paralabral cyst forms and what the cleft at the labral base represents.

exam2.question: A 62-year-old man has a painless thigh mass that has grown over three months. Sonography shows an 8 cm heterogeneous solid mass deep to the fascia with internal vascularity. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassurance and follow-up sonography in one year
MRI and referral to a sarcoma center before any biopsy

exam2.explanation: Size over 5 cm, deep location, growth, and internal vascularity are red flags for soft tissue sarcoma, so MRI and specialist referral with planned biopsy are appropriate. Unplanned excision can contaminate tissue planes and compromise later surgery.
exam2.hint: Count the red flags and consider why the sequence of interventions matters.

exam2.question: During an injection through thick subcutaneous fat into muscle, the straight needle appears bent at the fat-muscle interface. What explains this appearance?

options.text: Side-lobe artifact from the needle tip
Speed-of-sound difference between fat and muscle (bayonet artifact)
Mirror artifact from the muscle fascia

exam2.explanation: Sound travels more slowly in fat than in soft tissue, so the scanner miscalculates depth and the needle appears displaced at the interface, the bayonet artifact. A needle truly bending from bone contact would occur at the bone surface.
exam2.hint: Consider what is different about the two tissues on either side of the apparent bend.

exam2.question: A 24-year-old skier had a forced dorsiflexion injury and now has painful lateral ankle snapping. During active eversion, both peroneal tendons slide anterior to the lateral malleolus, and a small echogenic cortical fragment lies at the posterolateral fibula. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Superior peroneal retinaculum injury with peroneal tendon dislocation
Peroneus longus rupture at the cuboid tunnel
Intrasheath peroneal subluxation with intact retinaculum

exam2.explanation: Stripping of the superior peroneal retinaculum from the fibula, sometimes with a small cortical avulsion, allows the peroneal tendons to dislocate anteriorly during eversion and dorsiflexion. Intrasheath subluxation involves the tendons switching positions within an intact groove.
exam2.hint: Identify what normally holds the tendons in the retromalleolar groove.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old rock climber felt a pop in the ring finger during a crimp grip. With resisted flexion, sonography shows the flexor tendons lifting away from the proximal phalanx, with an increased tendon-to-bone distance compared with the adjacent finger. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Rupture of the A2 pulley, the most commonly injured pulley in climbers, allows the flexor tendons to bowstring away from the proximal phalanx, and dynamic resisted flexion accentuates the increased tendon-to-bone distance. A1 stenosing tenosynovitis causes triggering rather than bowstringing.
exam2.hint: Increased distance between the tendons and the proximal phalanx means a restraint at that level has failed.

exam2.question: A 46-year-old woman has burning pain and paresthesias in the sole of the foot. Sonography behind the medial malleolus shows a lobulated anechoic cyst beneath the flexor retinaculum displacing an enlarged nerve that lies between the flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus tendons. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Tarsal tunnel syndrome from ganglion compression of the tibial nerve
Baxter nerve entrapment by the abductor hallucis
Sural nerve compression at the lateral malleolus

exam2.explanation: The tibial nerve runs in the tarsal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum with the posterior tibial vessels, between the flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus; space-occupying lesions such as ganglia cause tarsal tunnel syndrome. The sural nerve is lateral.
exam2.hint: Identify the nerve that lies between the flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus at this level.

exam2.question: A solid, homogeneous hypoechoic nerve sheath tumor shows posterior acoustic enhancement. What is the most important lesson from this finding?

options.text: Posterior enhancement always indicates simple fluid
Posterior enhancement does not prove a lesion is cystic, so Doppler and compressibility should be used
Posterior enhancement occurs only behind calcified masses

exam2.explanation: Homogeneous solid lesions such as schwannomas and some lymphomas can show posterior enhancement, so internal Doppler flow and other features should be checked before calling a lesion a cyst. Calcified masses cast shadows instead.
exam2.hint: Consider what determines posterior enhancement and whether solid tissue can share that property.

exam2.question: A 41-year-old man developed sudden severe shoulder pain one week after a viral illness. As the pain subsided, weakness of abduction and external rotation followed. Sonography shows diffusely hyperechoic, slightly small supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles with intact tendons and no cyst along the suprascapular nerve course. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Suprascapular notch ganglion compressing the nerve
Adhesive capsulitis in the freezing phase

exam2.explanation: Acute severe pain followed by weakness after a viral illness, with denervation changes in suprascapular-innervated muscles and no compressive lesion, is typical of neuralgic amyotrophy. A compressive ganglion would be visible as a cyst at the notch.
exam2.hint: Consider the sequence of pain then weakness, and the lack of a structural compressive lesion.

exam2.question: A 25-year-old soccer player sustained a valgus injury. Sonography shows a thickened, hypoechoic medial collateral ligament with fibers that remain continuous, most pronounced near its femoral attachment, and no abnormal gapping on valgus stress. Which description best fits?

options.text: Complete MCL rupture at the tibial attachment
Low-grade MCL sprain, most often involving the proximal femoral portion

exam2.explanation: A thickened, hypoechoic ligament with continuous fibers and no instability is a low-grade sprain, and the proximal femoral portion is the most commonly injured site. A complete rupture would show fiber discontinuity and increased joint gapping on valgus stress.
exam2.hint: Continuous fibers and stable stress testing argue against the highest grade.

exam2.question: A 20-year-old woman inverted her ankle playing basketball. To best stretch and display the anterior talofibular ligament from the lateral malleolus to the talus, how should the foot be positioned?

options.text: Neutral with the foot hanging off the table

exam2.explanation: Plantar flexion and slight inversion tighten the anterior talofibular ligament, reducing anisotropy and making tears easier to see. Dorsiflexion is used to tighten the calcaneofibular ligament instead.
exam2.hint: Consider the course of the ligament from the fibula to the talus and which position puts it under tension.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old man with high-arched feet and a family history of similar problems has slowly progressive distal weakness. Sonography shows markedly and uniformly enlarged median, ulnar, and tibial nerves along their entire course, not only at entrapment sites. Which condition is most consistent?

options.text: Hereditary demyelinating neuropathy such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A
Diabetic mononeuropathy of the median nerve
Traumatic neuroma of the ulnar nerve

exam2.explanation: Diffuse, uniform enlargement of multiple nerves along their whole length is typical of CMT1A, consistent with the family history and pes cavus. Entrapment neuropathies produce focal enlargement at specific tunnels.
exam2.hint: Distinguish a generalized from a focal pattern of nerve enlargement.

exam2.question: A 28-year-old man with café-au-lait spots has a fusiform mass along the ulnar nerve. Sonography shows the nerve entering and exiting the center of the mass, which has a hyperechoic center and hypoechoic periphery. Which diagnosis is most likely?
exam2.explanation: In a patient with signs of neurofibromatosis type 1, a central fusiform mass inseparable from the nerve, with a target appearance, favors neurofibroma. A target sign can also occur in schwannoma, but schwannomas are typically eccentric.
exam2.hint: Note where the nerve enters and exits the mass relative to its center.

exam2.question: A 24-year-old soccer player felt a sharp pain in the posterior thigh while sprinting. Sonography of the biceps femoris shows a hypoechoic defect with fluid involving about one third of the muscle cross-section at the myotendinous junction, with no retraction. How is this strain best graded?
exam2.explanation: A visible fiber defect with fluid involving part of the muscle cross-section, without full discontinuity or retraction, is a grade 2 partial tear. Grade 1 shows edema without a defect, and grade 3 is complete with retraction.
exam2.hint: Ask whether fibers are disrupted and whether the disruption is complete.

exam2.question: A 5-year-old girl has a limp one week after an upper respiratory infection. A hip effusion is found. The referring physician asks whether the fluid character on ultrasound can distinguish transient synovitis from septic arthritis. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Septic effusions are always larger than transient synovitis effusions
Echogenicity of the fluid cannot reliably distinguish them, and clinical and laboratory findings or aspiration are required

exam2.explanation: Both septic and sterile effusions can be anechoic or echogenic, so sonography detects fluid and guides aspiration but cannot characterize infection. Relying on anechoic fluid to exclude infection is a dangerous pitfall.
exam2.hint: Ask whether fluid appearance is a sensitive or specific marker of infection.

exam2.question: A 14-year-old boy felt pain at the front of the pelvis while sprinting. Sonography shows a displaced cortical fragment from the anterior superior iliac spine with surrounding hematoma. Which muscle's pull most likely caused this avulsion?
exam2.explanation: The sartorius (with the tensor fasciae latae) originates at the anterior superior iliac spine and can avulse its apophysis in adolescent sprinters. The rectus femoris direct head avulses the anterior inferior iliac spine instead.
exam2.hint: Distinguish the superior from the inferior anterior iliac spine and the muscles attached to each.

exam2.question: A 19-year-old weightlifter has a painful snap at the medial elbow during flexion. Dynamic imaging shows the ulnar nerve dislocating anterior to the medial epicondyle, followed by the medial head of the triceps snapping over the epicondyle at deeper flexion. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Isolated ulnar nerve subluxation without muscle displacement
Anconeus epitrochlearis compressing the ulnar nerve
Medial epicondylitis with common flexor tendon tear
Snapping triceps syndrome with ulnar nerve dislocation

exam2.explanation: Two snaps during flexion, the ulnar nerve first and then the medial head of the triceps, define snapping triceps syndrome, which matters for surgical planning. Isolated nerve subluxation involves only the nerve.
exam2.hint: Count the structures that move over the epicondyle during flexion.

exam2.question: A 58-year-old woman with diabetes reports locking of the ring finger in flexion. Sonography at the metacarpal head shows a thickened hypoechoic pulley with hyperemia, and dynamic flexion shows the flexor tendons catching beneath it. Which pulley is most likely involved?
exam2.explanation: Stenosing tenosynovitis (trigger finger) results from thickening of the A1 annular pulley at the metacarpophalangeal joint level. The A2 pulley lies over the proximal phalanx and is more often torn in climbers than thickened.
exam2.hint: Note the level of the abnormality: over the metacarpal head.

exam2.question: A 19-year-old ballet dancer has a painful clunk in the anterior groin when bringing the hip from flexion, abduction, and external rotation back to extension. Dynamic sonography with the transducer over the superior pubic ramus, lateral to the femoral vessels, shows a tendon abruptly snapping from lateral to medial over the bone. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: External snapping hip from the iliotibial band
Intra-articular snapping from a labral tear
Snapping of the rectus femoris reflected head
Internal snapping hip from the iliopsoas tendon

exam2.explanation: Internal (iliopsoas) snapping hip is confirmed by an abrupt jerky movement of the iliopsoas tendon during return from the frog-leg position to extension. External snapping occurs laterally over the greater trochanter.
exam2.hint: Identify the tendon that crosses the anterior pelvic brim deep to the femoral neurovascular bundle.

exam2.question: A 50-year-old recreational runner has morning stiffness and pain in the back of the ankle. Sonography shows fusiform hypoechoic thickening of the Achilles tendon to 9 mm in AP dimension, centered 2 to 6 cm above the insertion, with neovessels entering from the ventral side. Why is this region typically affected?

options.text: It is where the plantaris tendon inserts
It is the site of the retrocalcaneal bursa
It is the relatively hypovascular zone of the tendon
It is the enthesis fibrocartilage region

exam2.explanation: Midportion Achilles tendinopathy occurs 2 to 6 cm above the insertion, in a zone of relatively poor blood supply. The retrocalcaneal bursa and the enthesis are at the insertion, which is the site of insertional tendinopathy.
exam2.hint: Consider blood supply along the length of the tendon.

exam2.question: A 71-year-old woman with hip osteoarthritis has groin fullness and leg swelling. Venous duplex shows no thrombus, but a large anechoic collection lies medial to the iliopsoas tendon at the level of the femoral head, compressing the femoral vein and connecting by a neck to the hip joint. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Iliopsoas bursitis communicating with the hip joint

exam2.explanation: The iliopsoas bursa lies anterior to the hip joint beside the iliopsoas tendon and communicates with the joint in a minority of adults; arthritis can distend it enough to compress the femoral vein. A pseudoaneurysm would show swirling arterial flow with a neck to the artery.
exam2.hint: Trace where the collection connects; its communication identifies its origin.

exam2.question: In a 47-year-old woman with forefoot pain, sonography shows an intermetatarsal lesion. Which feature favors intermetatarsal bursitis over Morton neuroma?

options.text: A solid hypoechoic lesion plantar to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament
A compressible fluid-containing lesion located dorsal to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament
Continuity of the lesion with the common plantar digital nerve
Reproduction of a Mulder click during forefoot squeezing

exam2.explanation: Intermetatarsal bursae lie dorsal to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament and are compressible with fluid, whereas Morton neuromas are solid, noncompressible, plantar to the ligament, and continuous with the digital nerve. The two can coexist, but their position relative to the ligament helps separate them.
exam2.hint: Use the deep transverse metatarsal ligament as the dividing landmark.

exam2.question: A sonographer is scanning a 61-year-old man with suspected rotator cuff tear and wants to focus on the region where most degenerative full-thickness supraspinatus tears begin. Where should attention be concentrated?

options.text: Posterior infraspinatus at the musculotendinous junction
Anterior distal supraspinatus, about 1 to 1.5 cm posterior to the biceps tendon
Superior border of the subscapularis near the coracoid
Teres minor insertion at the inferior facet

exam2.explanation: Degenerative tears classically begin in the anterior supraspinatus near its insertion, roughly 1 to 1.5 cm posterior to the long head biceps tendon, at the rotator crescent. Isolated tears of the infraspinatus or teres minor are uncommon.
exam2.hint: Use the intra-articular biceps tendon as the landmark for the anterior edge of the cuff region at risk.

exam2.question: A 36-year-old woman who recently had a baby has pain over the radial styloid with a positive Finkelstein test. Sonography shows thickened tendons with sheath fluid and a thickened overlying retinaculum at the radial styloid. Which tendons are involved?

options.text: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis

exam2.explanation: De Quervain tenosynovitis involves the first dorsal compartment, which contains the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis at the radial styloid. The radial wrist extensors form the second compartment.
exam2.hint: Consider which tendons are stretched when the thumb is flexed into the palm and the wrist is deviated ulnarly.

exam2.question: A 58-year-old woman with lateral hip pain has a fluid collection overlying the posterior facet of the greater trochanter, deep to the gluteus maximus and iliotibial band. Which structure is distended?
exam2.explanation: The trochanteric bursa lies over the posterior facet, deep to the gluteus maximus and iliotibial band, and is the largest peritrochanteric bursa. The subgluteus medius bursa lies deep to the gluteus medius over the lateral facet.
exam2.hint: Use the posterior facet and the overlying gluteus maximus to identify the bursa.

exam2.question: At the ischial tuberosity, which two muscles normally form the conjoint hamstring tendon?

options.text: Long head of the biceps femoris and semitendinosus
Short head of the biceps femoris and semimembranosus
Adductor magnus and long head of the biceps femoris

exam2.explanation: The conjoint tendon arises from the posteromedial ischial tuberosity and is formed by the semitendinosus and the long head of the biceps femoris; the semimembranosus has a separate anterolateral origin. The short head of the biceps femoris arises from the femur.
exam2.hint: One hamstring has its own separate footprint on the tuberosity; exclude it.

exam2.question: A 36-year-old man with recent weight gain who wears a heavy tool belt has burning numbness over the anterolateral thigh without weakness. Sonography shows a swollen hypoechoic nerve just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine as it passes under the inguinal ligament. Which nerve is affected?
exam2.explanation: Meralgia paresthetica is entrapment of the purely sensory lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the anterior superior iliac spine, often from tight belts or obesity. Femoral nerve lesions cause quadriceps weakness.
exam2.hint: Map the area of numbness to its nerve and the point where a belt could compress it.

exam2.question: A 34-year-old woman has posterior heel pain aggravated by rigid shoe counters. Sonography shows a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity, a distended retrocalcaneal bursa, a superficial calcaneal bursa, and insertional Achilles thickening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Haglund syndrome combines a prominent posterosuperior calcaneus, retrocalcaneal and superficial calcaneal bursitis, and insertional Achilles tendinopathy, often provoked by shoe counters. Sever disease is calcaneal apophysitis in children.
exam2.hint: The bony prominence plus shoe pressure is the key combination.

exam2.question: A 29-year-old skier has posterolateral knee pain and instability. Sonography shows a small bony fragment avulsed from the fibular head attached to the conjoined insertion of the lateral collateral ligament and biceps femoris. Which adjacent structure should be evaluated closely?
exam2.explanation: Fibular head avulsion indicates posterolateral corner injury, and the common peroneal nerve wraps around the fibular neck right next to it and is often injured. The pes anserine and saphenous nerve are medial structures.
exam2.hint: Consider which nerve lies closest to the fibular head and neck.

exam2.question: A 46-year-old woman wakes with severe shoulder pain without trauma. Sonography shows an ill-defined, amorphous, mildly echogenic deposit within the supraspinatus with no posterior shadowing, surrounding power Doppler hyperemia, and fluid in the subacromial bursa. Which stage of disease is most likely?

options.text: Chronic calcific bursitis in the resting phase

exam2.explanation: Soft, poorly marginated, nonshadowing calcium with hyperemia and acute pain is typical of the resorptive phase, which is when deposits are most amenable to lavage. Formative-phase deposits are hard, well defined, and cast a strong shadow.
exam2.hint: Link the acuity of pain and the lack of shadowing to the consistency of the calcium.

exam2.question: During a steep in-plane injection of the subacromial bursa, the needle is poorly seen. Which adjustment most improves needle visibility?

options.text: Increase the needle insertion angle so it is more vertical
Make the needle more parallel to the transducer face, or steer the beam so it strikes the needle closer to perpendicular
Increase the transducer frequency and decrease the gain

exam2.explanation: A needle reflects best as a specular reflector when the beam strikes it near 90 degrees, so a shallower insertion angle or beam steering improves visibility. Steeper angles and thinner needles make it harder to see.
exam2.hint: Consider how the angle between the beam and the needle affects how much echo returns to the transducer.

exam2.question: A 48-year-old man had a lumbar disc herniation with L5 radiculopathy two years ago and still has weakness of ankle dorsiflexion. Which sonographic finding in the tibialis anterior muscle best reflects chronic denervation?

options.text: Decreased echogenicity with increased muscle bulk
A normal echotexture with a focal hematoma
Increased echogenicity with reduced muscle bulk

exam2.explanation: Chronically denervated muscle undergoes atrophy and fatty infiltration, appearing smaller and hyperechoic with loss of the normal perimysial pattern. Acute strain causes hypoechoic edema rather than chronic hyperechoic atrophy.
exam2.hint: Consider what replaces muscle fibers after long-standing denervation.

exam2.question: A 66-year-old woman has chronic lateral hip pain and a Trendelenburg gait. Which sonographic finding indicates a full-thickness gluteus medius tear rather than tendinopathy?

options.text: A bare lateral facet with a fluid-filled tendon gap and a retracted tendon stump
Diffuse hypoechoic tendon thickening with continuous fibers
Fluid in the subgluteus maximus bursa over the posterior facet
Small enthesophytes at the facet with an intact tendon

exam2.explanation: A full-thickness gluteus medius tear appears as a tendon gap that leaves the facet uncovered (bare), with a retracted stump and often fluid filling the defect. Thickening with continuous fibers and enthesophytes indicate tendinopathy, and trochanteric bursal fluid can accompany either.
exam2.hint: Separate a change in tendon quality from loss of tendon coverage of the bone.

exam2.question: A 48-year-old woman has sharp medial heel pain with the first steps in the morning. Long-axis sonography shows a hypoechoic plantar fascia at its calcaneal origin. Which measurement best supports plantar fasciitis?

options.text: Fascia thickness greater than 2 mm in the midfoot
Fascia thickness less than 3 mm at the calcaneal origin
Fascia thickness equal to the contralateral side
Fascia thickness greater than 4 mm at the calcaneal origin

exam2.explanation: A plantar fascia thicker than about 4 mm at the medial calcaneal tubercle, often hypoechoic, is the widely used sonographic criterion for plantar fasciitis. Normal fascia is thinner, and midfoot abnormalities suggest fibromatosis rather than fasciitis.
exam2.hint: Recall the commonly used thickness cutoff and the site at which it is measured.

exam2.question: A 74-year-old man with long-standing shoulder weakness presents with a soft, fluctuant mass over the top of the shoulder. Sonography shows a large anechoic cyst above the acromioclavicular joint communicating through the joint with the glenohumeral space, and the supraspinatus is absent. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Acromioclavicular joint cyst from a chronic massive rotator cuff tear (geyser phenomenon)
Distal clavicular osteolysis with soft tissue edema
Paralabral cyst from a superior labral tear

exam2.explanation: With a chronic massive cuff tear, glenohumeral fluid escapes into the subacromial space and through a degenerated acromioclavicular capsule, forming a superficial cyst, the geyser phenomenon. A lipoma is solid and compressible, without communication with the joint.
exam2.hint: Trace the pathway joint fluid could take once the cuff no longer seals the glenohumeral joint.

exam2.question: A 58-year-old woman has medial knee pain. Coronal sonography shows the body of the medial meniscus extending 4 mm beyond the tibial plateau margin, with marginal osteophytes. Which association is most likely?

options.text: Medial meniscal posterior root tear and osteoarthritis

exam2.explanation: Medial meniscal extrusion greater than about 3 mm is abnormal and is strongly associated with meniscal root tears, degeneration, and osteoarthritis, because loss of hoop strength lets the meniscus displace. MCL sprains do not by themselves cause meniscal extrusion.
exam2.hint: Extrusion reflects loss of circumferential hoop restraint.

exam2.question: A 23-year-old volleyball player has anterior knee pain with jumping. Sonography shows focal hypoechoic thickening of the deep posterior fibers of the proximal patellar tendon at the inferior patellar pole, with neovascularity extending from the fat pad. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Jumper's knee is a tendinopathy of the proximal patellar tendon, classically affecting the deep posterior fibers at the inferior pole with neovascularity. Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease is an apophysitis of the inferior pole in skeletally immature children.
exam2.hint: Consider the patient's age and whether the abnormality is in the tendon or the growth center.

exam2.question: A 21-year-old baseball pitcher has medial elbow pain and reduced velocity. With dynamic valgus stress, the medial joint space widens more than on the asymptomatic side, and a thick band lying deep to the flexor-pronator mass is discontinuous at its distal attachment on the coronoid process. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Ulnar collateral ligament tear at the sublime tubercle
Ulnar nerve subluxation at the cubital tunnel

exam2.explanation: Repetitive valgus load in throwers injures the anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament, and a distal tear at the sublime tubercle is confirmed by ligament discontinuity and increased gapping under valgus stress compared with the other side. Common flexor tendon injury lies more superficially and does not produce joint gapping.
exam2.hint: Ask which structure deep to the flexor-pronator mass resists valgus opening of the medial elbow.

exam2.question: A 52-year-old woman has burning pain radiating to the third and fourth toes, worse in narrow shoes. Sonography from the plantar side shows an ovoid hypoechoic mass in the third intermetatarsal space between the metatarsal heads, and lateral squeezing of the forefoot produces a palpable click as the mass displaces plantarly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: A noncompressible hypoechoic mass in the third intermetatarsal space with a sonographic Mulder click is characteristic of Morton neuroma, a perineural fibrosis of the common plantar digital nerve. Bursitis is typically compressible and lies more dorsally.
exam2.hint: Weigh the intermetatarsal space involved and the response of the lesion to lateral forefoot compression.

exam2.question: A 22-year-old competitive rower has dorsal forearm pain and crepitus about 6 cm proximal to Lister tubercle. Sonography shows peritendinous edema where the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis cross over the radial wrist extensors. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Intersection syndrome is friction tenosynovitis where the first-compartment tendons cross the second-compartment tendons, typically 4 to 8 cm proximal to Lister tubercle, common in rowers. De Quervain tenosynovitis occurs more distally at the radial styloid.
exam2.hint: Locate the pain relative to Lister tubercle and the radial styloid.

exam2.question: A 16-year-old sprinter felt a sudden pop in the buttock during a race. Sonography at the ischial tuberosity shows a displaced curvilinear echogenic fragment with posterior shadowing, attached to the hamstring tendons, separated from the tuberosity by hypoechoic hematoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Myositis ossificans of the biceps femoris

exam2.explanation: In skeletally immature athletes, the apophysis is weaker than the tendon, so forceful hamstring contraction avulses a bony fragment from the ischial tuberosity. Myositis ossificans would develop weeks after injury, not as an acute displaced fragment.
exam2.hint: Consider which part of the muscle-tendon-bone unit is weakest before skeletal maturity.

exam2.question: A 45-year-old man has posterior ankle pain after a push-off injury, and the Achilles midportion shows a hypoechoic abnormal segment. Which dynamic finding indicates that the tendon is at least partly in continuity?

options.text: Fibers proximal and distal to the abnormal segment move together during gentle passive ankle motion
A hematoma-filled gap that widens with passive dorsiflexion
Herniation of Kager fat into the defect
Refractive shadowing arising from frayed tendon ends

exam2.explanation: Continuity is shown when fibers on both sides of the abnormal segment move together with gentle passive ankle motion. In a complete rupture the ends move independently, the gap widens with dorsiflexion, Kager fat may herniate into the defect, and refractive shadowing arises at the retracted ends.
exam2.hint: Compare how the two halves of a cut rope behave with how an intact rope behaves when pulled.

exam2.question: A 51-year-old woman has a 6 mm calcific deposit in the supraspinatus causing persistent pain despite 4 months of physical therapy. The deposit is soft and only faintly shadowing. Which ultrasound-guided procedure is most appropriate?

options.text: Percutaneous needle lavage (barbotage) of the deposit
Suprascapular nerve block at the spinoglenoid notch

exam2.explanation: Ultrasound-guided barbotage fragments and aspirates refractory calcific deposits, usually followed by a subacromial corticosteroid injection. Hydrodilatation is used for adhesive capsulitis, not calcific tendinopathy.
exam2.hint: Match each procedure to the condition it treats.

exam2.question: When scanning the posteromedial knee for a popliteal (Baker) cyst, which anatomic relationship confirms the diagnosis?

options.text: A neck extending between the medial head of the gastrocnemius and the semimembranosus tendon
A neck extending between the lateral head of the gastrocnemius and the biceps femoris
Communication with the proximal tibiofibular joint
Location within the popliteal artery wall

exam2.explanation: A true popliteal cyst is a distended gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa, and its neck between those two tendons is the defining finding that distinguishes it from other popliteal masses. Cysts tracking to the proximal tibiofibular joint are a separate entity.
exam2.hint: Identify the two posteromedial structures that bracket the bursa.

exam2.question: A 35-year-old skier fell on an abducted thumb. Sonography of the thumb MCP joint shows a torn ulnar collateral ligament whose retracted stump lies proximal and superficial to the adductor aponeurosis, forming a rounded hypoechoic mass. What is the clinical significance?

options.text: It is a partial tear that will heal with thumb spica immobilization
It is a ganglion cyst that should be aspirated
It is an avulsed sesamoid that can be treated with buddy taping
It is a Stener lesion, which prevents healing and generally requires surgical repair

exam2.explanation: When the adductor aponeurosis becomes interposed between the torn ulnar collateral ligament and its insertion, a Stener lesion, the ligament cannot heal in place and surgery is usually indicated. A nondisplaced partial tear, by contrast, can be immobilized.
exam2.hint: Consider what lies between the ligament stump and its attachment site.

exam2.question: A 32-year-old runner has posterior ankle pain and palpable crepitus. Sonography shows a normal-thickness Achilles tendon with preserved fibrillar echotexture, but hypoechoic thickening of the tissue surrounding the tendon with peritendinous hyperemia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: The Achilles has no true synovial sheath; inflammation of its surrounding paratenon produces hypoechoic peritendinous thickening and hyperemia while the tendon itself stays normal. Midportion tendinopathy would show fusiform thickening and hypoechogenicity of the tendon itself.
exam2.hint: Note that the tendon is normal and only the surrounding envelope is abnormal.

exam2.question: A 26-year-old runner has exercise-related burning and numbness over the dorsum of the foot that spares the first web space. Sonography shows focal swelling of a small nerve where it passes through the crural fascia in the distal anterolateral leg, about 10 to 12 cm above the lateral malleolus, with a small fascial defect. Which nerve is involved?
exam2.explanation: The superficial peroneal nerve becomes subcutaneous by piercing the crural fascia in the distal anterolateral leg and supplies most of the dorsal foot, sparing the first web space. The deep peroneal nerve supplies the first web space, and it stays deep to the fascia in the anterior compartment.
exam2.hint: Map the dorsal foot sensory territories to the nerves that supply them and where each becomes subcutaneous.

exam2.question: A 22-year-old woman has a soft, bluish forearm mass that enlarges when the arm hangs down. Sonography shows a compressible lesion of multiple hypoechoic channels containing small echogenic foci with posterior shadowing, and slow venous flow appears on release of compression. No high-velocity arterial flow is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Venous malformations are compressible, enlarge with dependency, contain slow venous flow often seen only with compression release, and may contain shadowing phleboliths. An arteriovenous malformation is a high-flow lesion with arterialized waveforms and feeding arteries.
exam2.hint: Weigh the flow velocity, the change with arm position and what the shadowing foci could represent.

exam2.question: Percutaneous ultrasound-guided needle tenotomy (fenestration) for chronic tendinosis works mainly by which mechanism?

options.text: Dissolving intratendinous calcium deposits with saline lavage
Blocking the sensory nerves that supply the painful tendon
Removing the inflamed bursa that overlies the tendon
Creating controlled injury that stimulates a new healing response

exam2.explanation: Repeated needle passes through the abnormal tendon segment disrupt degenerated tissue and cause bleeding, which converts a chronic degenerative process into an acute healing response. Saline lavage of calcium is a different procedure (barbotage) used for calcific tendinopathy.
exam2.hint: Chronic tendinosis lacks an effective repair response; the procedure tries to restart one.

exam2.question: Which scanning approach is most sensitive for detecting a small glenohumeral joint effusion?

options.text: Anterior coronal scan of the supraspinatus with the arm in the Crass position
Coronal scan over the acromioclavicular joint with the arm at the side
Transverse scan of the subscapularis with the arm in internal rotation
Posterior transverse scan of the posterior recess with the arm in external rotation

exam2.explanation: Glenohumeral joint fluid collects in the posterior recess between the posterior labrum and infraspinatus, and external rotation shifts fluid posteriorly, making small effusions easier to see. A supraspinatus scan in the Crass position shows the cuff and subacromial bursa, not the joint recess.
exam2.hint: Look where the joint capsule has a dependent recess beneath the posterior cuff.

exam2.question: A 40-year-old jammed the tip of his middle finger while catching a ball. The distal phalanx now droops, and he cannot actively extend the distal interphalangeal joint. Which sonographic finding is most expected?

options.text: Thickened A1 pulley at the metacarpophalangeal joint
Disruption of the central slip at the base of the middle phalanx
Discontinuity of the terminal extensor tendon at the dorsal distal phalanx
Tear of the flexor digitorum profundus at the distal phalanx

exam2.explanation: Inability to extend the DIP joint with a drooping fingertip is a mallet finger, caused by disruption of the terminal extensor tendon at the dorsal base of the distal phalanx. Central slip injury at the middle phalanx causes a boutonniere deformity at the PIP joint, not a DIP extension loss.
exam2.hint: Match the joint that cannot be extended to the extensor component that inserts just beyond it.

exam2.question: A 68-year-old woman has groin pain with active hip flexion, such as getting into a car, one year after total hip arthroplasty. Sonography shows a thickened hypoechoic iliopsoas tendon with surrounding fluid where the tendon crosses an anterior edge of the acetabular cup that protrudes beyond the bony rim. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Iliopsoas impingement from acetabular cup overhang

exam2.explanation: An acetabular component that protrudes anteriorly can rub on the iliopsoas tendon, causing tendinopathy and bursal fluid with painful active flexion after arthroplasty. A gluteus medius tear causes lateral hip pain and abductor weakness, not anterior pain linked to hip flexion.
exam2.hint: Relate the painful motion to the tendon that crosses directly over the anterior acetabulum.

exam2.question: During a posterior knee examination, a small oval echogenic structure with posterior acoustic shadowing is seen within the lateral head of the gastrocnemius behind the lateral femoral condyle. The patient has no symptoms there. What is it most likely?

options.text: Loose body within a Baker cyst
Calcified plaque of the popliteal artery
Avulsion fragment from the posterior cruciate ligament

exam2.explanation: The fabella is a common sesamoid within the lateral gastrocnemius head, appearing as a smooth shadowing echogenic focus posterior to the lateral femoral condyle. A Baker cyst loose body would lie within fluid between the medial gastrocnemius and semimembranosus, on the medial side.
exam2.hint: Some normal sesamoid bones live inside tendons of the posterior knee.

exam2.question: A 45-year-old runner who received several corticosteroid injections for plantar fasciitis felt a sudden pop under the heel while running. Sonography shows discontinuity of the plantar fascia fibers about 2 cm distal to the calcaneal origin with a surrounding hypoechoic hematoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Repeated corticosteroid injections weaken the plantar fascia and predispose it to rupture, seen as fiber discontinuity with hematoma near the origin after an acute pop. Plantar fibromatosis forms well-defined nodules in the mid-fascia without acute discontinuity or hematoma.
exam2.hint: Link the injection history and the acute pop to a loss of fiber continuity.

exam2.question: In the posterior calf, which superficial structure is the most useful landmark for locating the sural nerve?
exam2.explanation: The sural nerve runs in the subcutaneous tissue of the posterior calf alongside the small saphenous vein, which can be found easily and followed toward the lateral malleolus. The great saphenous vein runs with the saphenous nerve on the medial leg instead.
exam2.hint: Choose a structure in the same subcutaneous plane that is easy to find with light transducer pressure.

exam2.question: A 36-year-old man with a very high LDL cholesterol level and a family history of early myocardial infarction has painless bilateral thickening of the back of both ankles. Sonography shows diffuse fusiform thickening of both Achilles tendons with scattered hypoechoic foci, preserved continuity, and little Doppler flow. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Gouty tophi within the Achilles tendons

exam2.explanation: Familial hypercholesterolemia causes lipid deposits in tendons, most often the Achilles, producing painless bilateral fusiform thickening with hypoechoic foci. Gouty tophi appear as hyperechoic aggregates and occur with hyperuricemia and inflammatory attacks, not with markedly elevated LDL.
exam2.hint: Connect the lipid laboratory result to a deposit within the tendon.

exam2.question: Before performing an ultrasound-guided musculoskeletal injection, what is the most appropriate step to reduce the risk of vascular injury?

options.text: Survey the planned needle path with color or power Doppler to identify vessels
Increase the overall gain so the needle and vessels appear brighter
Switch to an out-of-plane approach to shorten the needle path
Apply firm transducer pressure to compress vessels along the path

exam2.explanation: Scanning the planned trajectory with color or power Doppler identifies arteries and veins so the needle path can be adjusted to avoid them. Firm transducer pressure can collapse veins so they become invisible, making them easier to puncture rather than avoid.
exam2.hint: Use the tool that shows flowing blood before the needle enters the skin.

exam2.question: A 34-year-old swimmer has chronic superior shoulder pain without trauma. Long-axis sonography along the acromion, posterior to the acromioclavicular joint, shows a cortical gap with smooth, well-corticated margins and a hypoechoic cleft, and a similar gap is present on the asymptomatic side. Gentle pressure on the anterior acromion produces slight motion at the gap. What is the most likely diagnosis?
exam2.explanation: Os acromiale is failure of fusion of an acromial ossification center, which is normally complete by about age 25. It appears as a cortical gap in the acromion separate from and posterior to the acromioclavicular joint, with smooth corticated margins, is often bilateral, and can be mobile and contribute to impingement. An acute fracture follows trauma and has sharp, irregular margins with hematoma, and the acromioclavicular joint lies more medially between the acromion and the clavicle.
exam2.hint: Compare the margins and the opposite shoulder: is this an acute injury or a developmental finding?

exam2.question: A 38-year-old woman has exquisite pinpoint pain beneath the fingernail that worsens with cold exposure. High-frequency sonography shows a 4 mm well-defined hypoechoic nodule in the nail bed beneath the nail plate with marked internal vascularity and slight scalloping of the distal phalanx cortex. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath

exam2.explanation: A small, hypervascular, hypoechoic subungual nodule with cold sensitivity, point tenderness, and bony scalloping is classic for a glomus tumor. A digital mucous cyst is anechoic, avascular, and usually arises near the DIP joint dorsally rather than under the nail with marked flow.
exam2.hint: Consider the subungual lesion known for a triad of pain, cold sensitivity, and point tenderness.

exam2.question: A Spigelian hernia protrudes through which location?

options.text: Hesselbach triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
The femoral canal, below the inguinal ligament and medial to the femoral vein
The semilunar line at the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis, usually near the arcuate line
The umbilical ring in the midline of the anterior abdominal wall

exam2.explanation: A Spigelian hernia passes through the Spigelian aponeurosis along the semilunar line at the lateral margin of the rectus abdominis, most often near or below the arcuate line, and is often concealed beneath an intact external oblique aponeurosis. A defect in Hesselbach triangle defines a direct inguinal hernia.
exam2.hint: This hernia is typically interparietal, often hidden beneath an intact external oblique aponeurosis.

exam2.question: A 24-year-old skier has an acute hemarthrosis after a pivoting injury. Which posterior-approach sonographic finding is an indirect sign of an anterior cruciate ligament tear?

options.text: Anechoic fluid in the prepatellar bursa
Thickening of the pes anserinus tendons
A hypoechoic collection along the lateral wall of the intercondylar notch
Hypoechoic swelling of the semimembranosus insertion

exam2.explanation: The ACL attaches to the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle, so a tear often leaves a hypoechoic hematoma along the lateral wall of the intercondylar notch, seen from a posterior approach. Prepatellar bursal fluid is superficial and unrelated to cruciate injury.
exam2.hint: Think about where the ACL attaches on the femur.

exam2.question: In a patient with progressive collapsing flatfoot, which ligament lying deep to the posterior tibial tendon, extending from the sustentaculum tali to the navicular, should be evaluated?
exam2.explanation: The spring ligament supports the talar head from below, runs from the sustentaculum tali to the navicular deep to the posterior tibial tendon, and is often thickened or torn with posterior tibial tendon dysfunction and flatfoot. The bifurcate ligament lies on the dorsolateral midfoot and does not support the medial arch.
exam2.hint: Find the ligament that cradles the talar head on the medial side of the arch.

exam2.question: A 45-year-old woman had a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck. She now has a drooping shoulder, difficulty raising the arm above horizontal, and mild scapular winging. Sonography shows a thin, hyperechoic trapezius compared with the other side. Which nerve was most likely injured?
exam2.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially, where it is at risk during lymph node biopsy, and its injury denervates the trapezius. The long thoracic nerve also causes winging, but it supplies the serratus anterior and does not lie in the posterior triangle at the biopsy site.
exam2.hint: Match the atrophic muscle to its motor nerve and to where that nerve runs in the neck.

exam2.question: A 30-year-old has a painless, mobile oval lump in the groin. Sonography shows an oval hypoechoic structure with a central echogenic fatty hilum, central hilar vascularity, and a short-axis to long-axis ratio below 0.5. What does this most likely represent?
exam2.explanation: An oval shape, preserved echogenic fatty hilum, and central hilar flow are features of a benign or reactive lymph node, which is common in the groin. Metastatic nodes tend to be rounded with loss of the fatty hilum and peripheral or chaotic vascularity.
exam2.hint: Focus on the preserved central fatty structure and the oval shape.

exam2.question: Which practice is recommended for ultrasound-guided musculoskeletal injections to reduce the risk of infection?

options.text: Using ordinary bottle gel at the puncture site after an alcohol wipe of the transducer
Skin antisepsis with a sterile transducer cover and sterile gel at the puncture site
Cleaning the skin after the needle is inserted to avoid diluting anesthetic
Wiping the transducer with water between patients and using an uncovered probe

exam2.explanation: Aseptic technique for guided injections includes skin antisepsis (such as chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine), a sterile transducer cover, and sterile single-use gel where the needle enters. Nonsterile bottle gel at the puncture site has been linked to contamination and infection, even if the probe is wiped.
exam2.hint: Everything that touches the puncture site should be sterile.
